articles.title: Former GitHub CEO launches rival platform built for AI coding agents
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A startup led by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is introducing its own platform for storing, reviewing and shipping code written by AI agents, competing with the company he used to run.

The startup, Entire , on Monday unveiled what it calls a Git forge — a service for hosting code, reviewing changes and running builds, the core of what GitHub does — designed for teams whose AI agents write code faster than people can review it. The company is pitching it as an alternative to GitHub.
The news comes two days before GitHub’s annual Universe conference in San Francisco. Microsoft acquired GitHub for $7.5 billion in 2018 and has since folded it into its CoreAI division.

The biggest change is Trails, Entire’s replacement for the pull request, the standard way developers propose and review code changes. The pull request “has become an audit log that only the agent reads,” Dohmke wrote in a blog post Monday. Instead of reading through every changed line, developers see a dashboard of scores from AI agents evaluating the code on each update.

According to Entire, multiple AI agents check the quality of each change, so developers can merge code without reading every line. Teams can also require a person’s sign-off, or passing automated tests, before any code goes in, the company said.

The launch comes as GitHub strains under the load from AI agents. The platform has had several significant outages in recent months, including one in August that lasted nearly eight hours. GitHub is moving from its own data centers to Microsoft’s Azure cloud to add capacity. GitHub said developers and agents made 7.38 billion commits, or saved code changes, on the platform in September alone.
Dohmke, who is based in Bellevue, Wash., left GitHub last year after nearly four years as CEO. Entire says it now has 50 employees. The company is fully remote.

Entire isn’t alone in rethinking code hosting for AI agents. AI coding company Cursor launched its own code-hosting service , Origin, in August. And Anthropic recently described building its own source control system as the number of code changes it merged each day grew from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September.

With the latest updates, Entire now lets developers host private code repositories directly on its service in the U.S., Europe, India and Australia, and says its service can handle up to 89 times as many code pushes per second as GitHub, based on its own benchmarks. It’s partnering with Buildkite and Depot on build and test pipelines, giving developers a way to move off GitHub Actions. Public repositories and self-hosting are on the roadmap.

Entire is also adding what it calls Continuous Memory, which lets AI agents search past coding sessions for the context behind earlier changes. The company says one part of it, a map of the codebase, cut token use by up to 71% in its testing.

That goes beyond the startup’s July launch , which mirrored existing GitHub repositories on a faster network rather than replacing them. Developers can still mirror from GitHub, or now move their code to Entire instead.

Microsoft’s venture arm M12 was among the backers of Entire’s $60 million seed round in February. Felicis led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona and Basis Set Ventures, along with individual investors such as Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

“Code review was always a bottleneck,” Dohmke said at a Madrona event last month. “I’ve never worked in a software company where I didn’t wait for somebody else to review my pull request, and you have to ping people in Slack three times. And there was this one guy that had to review everything because he knew what to look for. And now that bottleneck is 10 times bigger.”

articles.title: Microsoft makes new ‘voluntary exit’ offer to about a quarter of its workforce, including some execs
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft is making a new buyout offer to a much broader group of employees, this time including some executives — signaling that it’s not done shrinking its workforce despite thousands of layoffs and retirements this year.

The Voluntary Exit Offer, announced Monday in a memo to employees, is open to about 60,000 people in participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India, the company told GeekWire. That’s about a quarter of its workforce, which numbered 223,000 people at last count.

Microsoft didn’t provide a projection for how many employees will accept, but the company told GeekWire it anticipates a much smaller share than the roughly 30% who took its earlier voluntary retirement offer, which went to longtime employees more likely to take the deal.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” wrote Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s chief people officer, in the memo to employees.
It also gives participating organizations within the company “another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” she added.
Microsoft’s count of 223,000 full-time employees as of June 30 was down from 228,000 a year earlier, according to its annual filings. That latest number came before its July layoffs.
However, Microsoft says the offer isn’t a sign that it needs fewer employees. Instead, a company spokesperson described it as one of several ways it’s adjusting to changing business needs.
The Voluntary Exit Offer includes financial support and career planning resources, according to the memo. It says eligible employees will receive the details by email.

The package is equivalent to Microsoft’s standard severance, according to the company, including base pay based on tenure and level, continued stock vesting, healthcare coverage for a fixed period and career transition services. It doesn’t include the extended healthcare that was a major draw of the retirement program. Employees have until the first week of December to decide.

The new offer does not come with any age or tenure requirement, and performance isn’t a factor, the company said. It goes up to level 70 on Microsoft’s internal scale, which includes general managers and some employees with vice president titles, but not corporate vice presidents.

That’s a big change from the voluntary retirement program that Microsoft offered this spring, which was the first in its history. That program was limited to U.S. employees at the senior director level (level 67) and below whose age plus years at the company reached a minimum threshold. The company described that as a one-time initiative.
Buyouts are still relatively rare among the largest tech companies, which have generally relied on layoffs, stricter performance reviews and return-to-office mandates to thin their ranks.
Like its peers, Microsoft is under pressure from Wall Street to hold down operating expenses as it pours tens of billions of dollars into data centers and AI infrastructure.

Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs in July , about 2% of its global workforce, including about 600 in Washington state, followed by hundreds more across the company in September. The company cut more than 15,000 jobs in 2025.
The company said the new offer is not a replacement for layoffs, which will remain part of the company’s approach depending on business conditions.

When Microsoft offered the retirement program this spring, about 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible U.S. employees took the deal . Coleman told GeekWire in July that the results reduced the size of the layoffs Microsoft announced that month.
At the time, Coleman said Microsoft was studying how to make voluntary exits a more regular part of how it manages its workforce, possibly on an annual or ongoing basis.

Among the other changes this time, Microsoft is leaving it to business leaders to decide whether their groups participate, the company said. The company’s sales organization is not participating, nor are some engineering groups and corporate functions.

“There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee,” Coleman wrote in the memo, explaining that participation by different groups “varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments, and workforce needs.”

She said Microsoft will keep helping employees build new skills and, where it makes sense, move into other jobs inside the company. Microsoft said in July that it had redeployed more than 4,000 employees into new roles over the previous year.

Microsoft reports quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon, which could include projections for the cost of the new buyout offer. The company disclosed a $900 million charge for the retirement program in its April earnings report.

articles.title: ‘Not a new AI center’: Seattle Children’s launches $10M pediatric innovation institute
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle Children’s is announcing today the launch of its Institute for Pediatric Innovation , a $10 million initiative with eight focus areas and a chief innovation officer yet to be named. The hospital is positioning the institute as the “core engine” driving its strategic plan.
CEO Dr. Christopher Longhurst has specific health challenges in mind where he hopes today’s technology could quickly improve care for pediatric patients.

“The question is, with this new generation of tools — not just AI and large language models, but precision health tools, whole genome sequencing, etc. — how can we leverage these tools to solve problems in ways that we have not before?” Longhurst said in an interview with GeekWire.

The institute “is not a new AI center. This isn’t about the shiny objects or the tools. This is about the outcomes that we can achieve and the impact that we can have,” Longhurst said. “So really, the focus here is impact at scale.”
Seattle Children’s has approximately 600,000 patient visits last year and reported approximately $2.6 billion in expenses.

Longhurst became CEO in January after a decade at UC San Diego Health, where he founded and directed the Joan & Irwin Jacobs Center for Health Innovation. The institute is Seattle Children’s most prominent new organization-wide initiative since he took the job.
The institute will concentrate on eight areas:

AI tools. Seattle Children’s plans to develop, test and use new technology tools. Longhurst said there is a need for a digital care platform specific to pediatric patients where families and providers can manage appointments, medications, results and communications. The hospital is already helping build one with industry partners and Longhurst is eager to include an AI chatbot for caregivers. Other AI work includes a pilot of an automated tool that rapidly generates anonymous copies of medical images for research and a listening tool that drafts clinical notes during appointments.

Industry partnerships. Longhurst said these cut across the other focus areas. The hospital is working with industry on the care platform, for example, and plans to partner on seeking FDA approval for pediatric uses of existing devices.

Innovation unit. The hospital is establishing a facility that offers advanced care and can test new pediatric devices. Longhurst pointed to Ochsner Health’s innovation lab as a model and said he wasn’t aware of a comparable facility focused on children.

Medical device innovation . This focus overlaps with the innovation care unit and aims to serve unmet pediatric needs. Longhurst noted that numerous medical devices designed for adults are being used off-label for children. One piece of the solution is taking data related to these applications and seeking FDA approval for use in kids.

Precision medicine. Seattle Children’s already offers targeted therapies and aims to expand them. A recently published study from the hospital found that genome analysis, usually performed only for critically ill patients, could lead to faster diagnoses for non-ICU patients, particularly children with failure to thrive. “The question for us now is … how do we make a research project into something that we do every day at scale?” Longhurst said.

Biomedical data. Patient monitoring produces vast amounts of electronic data that can be combined with genetic and protein-expression information. The hospital is pursuing technology that recognizes patterns across these sources in real time to guide treatment for critically ill and other patients.
Therapeutics. Research into next-generation cell, gene and protein therapies will expand.

Training for young scientists and clinicians. The hospital’s Invent@SC program provides mentorship and education for early-career researchers and clinicians. The initiative focuses on treatments discovered at Seattle Children’s that can be widely adopted.

Projects from the institute must be approved by a Seattle Children’s AI Review Board, which will assess whether proposed uses of AI are ethical, equitable and responsible. Those involving research will also go to the Institutional Review Board for regulatory compliance.

Seattle Children’s has recruited three external launch advisors to help recruit the CIO and develop the institute’s organizational structure. They are Dr. Matthew Lungren, a Stanford University adjunct professor and former chief scientific officer for health and life sciences at Microsoft; Dr. Kevin Koo, a radiologist whose experience includes leadership at Seattle Children’s and roles at UW Medicine and McKinsey & Company; and Dr. Jessica Mega, a cardiologist and co-founder of Verily, an Alphabet company.
Longhurst said the work will require a cultural shift at the institution, from risk aversion to openness to change.
The institute’s initial funding comes from a $5 million anonymous gift and $5 million in existing resources. Longhurst acknowledged the amount is limited relative to the scope of the work.
“That’s really just the beginning,” he said. “And what that should signify is a commitment from me as the leader to allocate actual investments in this space.”

articles.title: T-Mobile’s new ‘T-Mix’ plans let customers trade phone deals for Netflix, ESPN and other perks
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: T-Mobile is introducing new wireless plans that change how customers get perks and phone deals, giving them a set number of “Picks” to spend on a new phone or an expanded menu of extras that they can swap out every 90 days.

The company says it will be the only carrier that lets customers choose which benefits come with their plan. Instead of fixed bundles of extras plus a discount on a new phone for each line, customers get a single allowance to spend on options ranging from Netflix and ESPN to Xbox Game Pass, Google’s Gemini AI and Delta SkyMiles.
One catch is that phones and perks come out of the same pool of Picks, so a family that wants a new phone on every line may have little left to put toward extras.
The plans, called T-Mix, will be available in November. Existing customers can switch or keep their current plans, said Allan Samson, T-Mobile’s chief marketing officer.

The move comes as T-Mobile’s customer growth slows and new rivals emerge, including SpaceX, a current T-Mobile partner that is reportedly planning a wireless service of its own. T-Mobile’s stock is down about 26% this year , including a drop of nearly 8% on Friday after a report on SpaceX’s wireless plans.
The Bellevue, Wash.-based company has relied for years on “Un-carrier” moves — splashy changes that defy industry conventions — to capture consumer attention.

Samson described T-Mix as the latest of those moves, aimed at what the company’s research identified as a top customer complaint: paying for extras they don’t use. Picks are “essentially a form of currency,” he said. “You can use them for anything you want.”
A subscription hub: With the new plans, T-Mobile is adding a much larger menu of subscriptions in an attempt to turn its plans into a hub for streaming, music, gaming and AI services.

Along with longtime perks such as Netflix, Hulu and Apple TV, the new options include ESPN’s Unlimited streaming service, Xbox Game Pass, YouTube Premium, Apple Music and Google’s Gemini AI subscriptions.

The company says people spend far more on subscriptions than they realize. In T-Mobile’s research, customers estimated spending about $90 a month, Samson said. A separate study by C+R Research puts average spending at $219.

A big part of the idea is to consolidate that spending and let customers move among services more freely, picking up a streaming service for a new show, for example, or adding satellite coverage for a summer trip, then dropping it afterward.

Customers can make those changes every 90 days in the T-Life app. T-Mobile texts them when a 10-day change window opens, and their choices roll over if they do nothing. T-Mobile handles the switch between services in its plans, although the fine print notes that customers may need to initially cancel existing subscriptions on their own to avoid paying twice.

T-Mobile buys subscriptions below retail prices through deals it negotiates with streaming services and other partners. That lets T-Mobile include the services in its plans for less than it would cost customers to subscribe on their own.
Phones vs. perks: For consumers, one trade-off for the newfound flexibility is that phones and perks now draw from the same finite supply.

Customers who hold on to their phones or choose less-expensive models can put that value toward streaming and other extras, but a family that wants a new phone on every line may not have enough Picks to cover them.

Whether consumers end up getting more or less for their money depends largely on how many lines they have and how often they buy new phones. Smaller accounts that keep their phones are likely to come out ahead. Larger families that upgrade every line may pay more and get less, because T-Mobile is also dropping its long-standing free third line.

Samson estimated that accounts with one or two lines will pay $5 to $10 a month less than on T-Mobile’s current plans, while a five-line account might pay $10 to $15 more. Across all of its customers, he said, pricing is roughly the same.

T-Mobile says a family of three on its Loaded plan, which costs $200 a month ($2,400 a year) with AutoPay before taxes and fees, gets more than $4,320 a year in plan features and benefits, based on its own valuation.
The math behind the Picks: Customers choose from three plans, with base prices for customers on AutoPay, before taxes and fees:
Adding lines adds Picks, and Picks apply to the whole account, so one Netflix subscription covers the family. Unused Picks don’t accumulate from one quarter to the next.

Most extras cost one or two Picks. Ad-free Netflix costs three, and ESPN Unlimited costs four. Phones cost Picks, too: two for an iPhone and three for an iPhone Pro, Samson said, tied up for the three-year payment plan. A four-line account on the More plan gets seven Picks, not enough for a new iPhone on every line.

No price guarantee: The terms say T-Mobile may change the benefits and the number of Picks each one requires at any time, with changes taking effect the following quarter. Customers who change a partner benefit outside a change window may have to pay a fee. Once a year, customers will also be asked to reselect their benefits.

The launch comes less than a week after New York Attorney General Letitia James announced a settlement with T-Mobile over its 2017 “Price Guarantee” plans, which promised customers the carrier would “never change the price you pay.”

T-Mobile raised prices on those plans by about $5 a line in 2024. It agreed to offer refunds and other options that the attorney general’s office expects to provide more than $38 million in value, and to freeze prices for affected customers until at least 2029.

Asked about price protections, Samson said T-Mix plans don’t come with a guarantee. T-Mobile can control its network costs, he said, but not what partners such as Apple and Xbox charge, although it has multiyear deals in place.
“We didn’t want to be disingenuous,” he said, adding that partner prices are set for the next couple of years but “I can’t tell you what’s going to happen in 2030.”

The Un-carrier playbook: T-Mobile launched its Un-carrier campaign in 2013 by dropping two-year contracts. Samson said the company makes an Un-carrier move only when it sees a big customer pain point and believes it has something unique to offer.

T-Mobile has been testing T-Mix since Oct. 1 in 37 stores in Kansas City. Only about 70% of Picks were chosen in the store at the time of purchase, Samson said, in part because families wanted to go home and decide together, and some customers were saving Picks for phones coming out later.
Details of the plans leaked in recent weeks, first reported by The Mobile Report and later by PhoneArena .
Verizon lets customers add discounted streaming bundles to its plans for an extra monthly charge. Samson said the difference with T-Mix is that the benefits are included in the plan price.

Upholding the company’s tradition of jabbing at rivals, he described one competitor’s approach as “naked connectivity.” The other, he said, will “throw you a nice phone and then leave you alone. And every now and then, there’s a rate increase.”
The plans are also one of the first major consumer moves under CEO Srini Gopalan, who succeeded Mike Sievert in the role last November.

T-Mobile’s account growth has slowed this year. In the second quarter, it added a net 277,000 postpaid accounts (households and businesses that pay a monthly bill rather than prepaying for service). That was down 13% from 318,000 a year earlier .
The company reports third-quarter results Wednesday, two days after Verizon .
SpaceX is also reportedly seeking cell sites to build a rival wireless network, even though T-Mobile’s T-Satellite service runs on SpaceX’s Starlink .

Samson, who joined Sprint in 2016 and stayed on after its 2020 merger with T-Mobile, became CMO earlier this year. He previously ran the company’s broadband business and was CMO of T-Mobile for Business. He said T-Mix has been his pet project since taking his current role, starting with interviews with hundreds of consumers.

Samson said it’s too early to say how T-Mix will affect the business. “Ask me in six months once I have about six months under my wings nationwide,” he said, “and then we’ll have some actuals to report.”

articles.title: Most Puget Sound Cities Aren't Keeping Up With Housing Growth Targets
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A small number of cities across central Puget Sound are pulling along the entire region when it comes to keeping pace with long-term housing growth targets, according to new data released by the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC). Of the 40 cities across King, Pierce, Snohomish and Kitsap Counties that are expected to accommodate the largest share of regional housing growth through 2044, just 14 are on track and many are significantly behind.

The data provides a snapshot of uneven urban growth, more than a half-decade after a pivot in the four-county region's housing growth strategy toward transit investments that were either already in place or coming online. Though that strategy is clearly bearing some fruit, with cities like Shoreline, Redmond, and Mountlake Terrace easily dispatching with their targets, these numbers also point to the need for potential reforms around land use and building regulations elsewhere – some of which are already in motion.

"The region is producing housing at pace to meet its targets, but this is largely led by just a handful of jurisdictions," Eric Clute, a planner in PSRC's data department, said last week while breaking down the data for local elected officials. "I think these jurisdictions can offer a blueprint to others looking to boost production and meet their housing targets."

The adopted growth targets on the books right now across the urban areas of all four counties plan for a total of approximately 620,000 new units of housing by 2044, with close to half of that in King County. As a whole, the region has been outpacing that target, adding around 183,000 units since 2019 or 2020 – the start year varies by county, with the clock starting for King County in 2019, compared to 2020 for the other three counties.

That growth rate is around 16,000 more units than was needed to keep pace. But without growth in Seattle significantly outpacing its growth target – 70,000 units were built compared to a prorated growth target of just over 31,000 – the region as a whole would not be ahead of the overall target. Falling short will mean that Washington will likely fail to add the 1.1 million overall homes needed over the next two decades to tread water on housing affordability, according to the state's Commerce Department.

PSRC's Vision 2050 growth strategy lays out different tiers of jurisdictions expected to shoulder decreasing shares of regional housing growth. At the top are the metro cities, including Seattle, Tacoma, Bellevue, Everett, and Bremerton. These cities have the biggest growth targets, though a smaller overall target for Kitsap County means some cities across the Sound are aiming for more housing than Bremerton.

Out of those five, only Seattle outpaced its growth target, with Everett lagging the most. Snohomish County's largest city logged just over 2,000 new homes compared to an overall target of 36,500 by 2044. Bellevue did better , seeing more than 5,000 units built against a similar target. Tacoma saw more than 7,000 new units, but has an even more ambitious growth target of 43,000.

Just below those five big kahunas are the "core cities," mid-sized jurisdictions that are also expected to carry a significant amount of regional growth. Just four out of 15 of those cities – Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah and Kent – are meeting or exceeding their targets. Renton, Auburn and Federal are falling the furthest short, while Lynnwood and Bothell are doing better.

Outside of metro and core cities, another set of cities known as "high capacity transit (HCT) communities" are also planning for a fairly significant share of growth. HCT communities feature some type of current or future transit investments, from a Sounder commuter or Link light rail station to a planned bus rapid transit line.

Nine of those 20 cities are on track, with Shoreline leading the pack. Woodinville, Mountlake Terrace, and Port Orchard are other standouts here, with Edmonds falling significantly short of expectations. DuPont, which had been set to see an extension of Sound Transit's S Line until an agency board vote earlier this year through a construction timeline into limbo , saw essentially no housing growth at all.

The good news here is that required updates to local growth plans made by the end of 2024, along with required zoning adjustments to allow more types of housing in lower density neighborhoods the following year, are just starting to bear fruit. In the metro cities specifically, many of those adjustments were bold ones, including the Home in Tacoma rezones and Bellevue's land use code reforms that targeted areas ripe for redevelopment, like Wilburton .

"We have all made recent updates to Comprehensive Plans that made significant changes to spur housing production," Clute said. "These changes are likely not yet showing up in the data. Those changes were done just a couple years ago, or a year ago, and development takes several years to happen."

And then there are the cities and towns that are not expected to shoulder as much growth, places like North Bend, Gig Harbor, and Lake Stevens. Growth in those places, on the whole, has been significantly outpacing growth targets, a fact that stands in stark contrast with the bigger cities that are lagging behind.

What about urban unincorporated areas? Areas outside cities and towns but still inside the urban growth area (UGA) saw significant growth in Pierce County, and less growth in Snohomish and Kitsap Counties. King County's modest urban unincorporated growth target is right on pace.

Slower-than-expected growth in unincorporated Kitsap County is likely good news for urbanists, who have argued that the growth plans for those areas set up suburban sprawl . On the other hand, unincorporated Snohomish County includes areas set to see light rail expansion, including the vicinity of the Ash Way and Mariner Park and Ride stations being built as part of Everett Link .

Ultimately, the numbers released last week could represent a new baseline, with housing production in Seattle slowing significantly and overhauled zoning across Puget Sound potentially setting the stage for increased growth elsewhere. If Seattle's steady homebuilding pace falters without other cities picking up the slack, the region could be in for more housing affordability woes.

While underlying land use regulations clearly aren't the only factor at play when it comes to regional growth, they do play a big role. And though the region as a whole may be slightly ahead of the curve, that's no reason for any city to sit on its laurels.

articles.title: How the Crosslake Connection Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On March 28, Sound Transit opened the much anticipated Crosslake Connection. This rail connection between Seattle and cities on the Eastside promised fast, frequent, and more reliable connectivity across Lake Washington. The Link 2 Line was designed to replace the hundreds of daily bus trips on I-90, freeing up service hours to improve local bus routes. Initially, however, the I-90 bus routes remained intact to offer extra capacity and redundancy during the World Cup. In the five months following the Crosslake Connection opening, passengers could either take the train or bus. Many chose to take the train. In August 2026, the 11 Link stations on the Eastside and Mercer Island accounted for 12,500 boardings each weekday.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in east King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.
Sound Transit Express routes 550 and 554 provided all-day bus service across Lake Washington via I-90. Following the full 2 Line opening, many people switched from one of these routes to Link.

Overall ridership on Route 550 dropped 52% year-over-year. Boardings at the route’s busiest stop in 2025, Bellevue Transit Center, fell 57% as many passengers opted to take the 2 Line instead. Along Bellevue Way, the stop at 4th Street took the crown as the busiest stop with 278 weekday boardings (this stop had 366 weekday boardings in 2025). The other stops on Bellevue Way did not see significant changes in ridership. One stop that saw an increase in passenger boardings is South Bellevue station for Bellevue-bound trips. Passengers transferring from the 2 Line to Route 550 to access a stop on Bellevue Way doubled the boarding count to 50 per day. Route 550 stops near South Bellevue station and Mercer Island station. Seattle-bound boardings on Route 550 at those stops dropped by 78% and 74%, respectively.

Similar to Route 550, ridership on Route 554 fell where it overlaps with Link but remained constant elsewhere. Route 554’s stops in Issaquah had similar ridership to 2025. However, boardings at the Eastgate P&R (I-90 & 142nd Pl) fell 42%. This is likely due to more people choosing to use the nearby South Bellevue P&R and Link instead. On Mercer Island, the number of passengers boarding a Route 554 bus dropped 72% as many switched to the 2 Line. Route 554 was replaced by Route 556 in August. Route 556 provides more frequent service between Issaquah and Bellevue, via South Bellevue station and Bellevue Way.

State Route 520 is the only other connection between Seattle and the Eastside across Lake Washington. Some bus routes that use SR-520, such as Route 255, do not complete with the 2 Line and saw negligible changes in ridership patterns following the 2 Line opening. Other routes had significant changes as some passengers switched to the Link 2 Line.

While Route 545 takes a different route from Link across Lake Washington, it offers redundant service with the 2 Line between Redmond and downtown Seattle. Following the full 2 Line opening, ridership on the route fell 20%. At SR-520 & 40th St (near Redmond Technology station), inbound boardings fell 19%. Likewise, boardings at Redmond Transit Center dropped by 23%.

In downtown Seattle, Route 545 ridership has shifted north. Stops along Olive Way had a collective 2.5% increase in boardings, despite the closure of the peak-only stop at Boren Ave. Meanwhile, stops on 4th Ave had a collective 36% decrease in passenger boardings. This reflects passengers choosing to take the fastest trip. Route 545 is often faster than Link between the Denny Triangle and Redmond, while Link is usually faster between Redmond and CID or Pioneer Square. After all, Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think .

Compared to the 2 Line, Route 542 offers a shortcut between Redmond and the U District. A trip from the U District to downtown Redmond on Link takes 56 minutes vs just 32 minutes via Route 542. Ridership on this route has remained steady, with a 2.4% increase in boardings year-over-year. There were no significant changes to the route’s ridership patterns.

Route 271 also connected Seattle with the Eastside via SR-520. The long route had several noticeable changes in its ridership patterns following the opening of the Crosslake Connection. Trips between the U District and downtown Bellevue take 37 minutes on Link vs 24 minutes on Route 271. Despite the faster trip time on Route 271, the number of passengers boarding Seattle-bound trips at Bellevue Transit Center dropped 47%. This is likely from passengers who previously connected to another route in the U District and now have a more time-competitive option with Link (eg: trips from Bellevue to Capitol Hill).
Route 271 also had a 41% decrease in boardings at Eastgate Park & Ride. This is the same changed observed with Route 554 and is likely to due more people using the South Bellevue P&R instead.

The only new 2 Line station in Seattle, Judkins Park, impacted the ridership patterns of the five King County Metro routes that stop nearby: routes 7, 8, 9, 48, and 106. The intersection of an east-west Link station and five north-south bus routes is a key opportunity for many transfers. However, the data show that only 486 people are transferring between Link and one of the bus routes each weekday. This accounts for about ⅓ of boardings at Judkins Park station, a bit less than the projected 42% . The table below breaks down the bus boardings at Judkins Park station by route and direction.

The Crosslake Connection is already making its mark on travel patterns across Lake Washington. Many passengers switched from routes 271, 545, 550, and 554 to Link when it was the faster option. In Seattle, fewer people than expected are transferring between buses and the 2 Line at Judkins Park station.

The five month period of overlapping Link and bus service has come to a close and many bus routes were truncated in August . Seattle Transit Blog will share ridership data analysis from those changes in Spring 2027 (when the data are available).

In the meantime, explore detailed ridership data for most King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Community Transit routes at seattletransitridership.com . The dashboard has been updated to include stop-level data for all Metro and Metro operated Sound Transit routes from the Spring 2026 service change. The impact of the Federal Way Link Extension on bus routes in south King County will be discussed in an article tomorrow.

articles.title: ‘For Ayşenur’ — Central District mural will honor UW activist killed by Israeli forces
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A new community mural honoring late University of Washington graduate and activist Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi is slated for installation on the grounds of Cherry Street Village in the Central District.
Permits with the city have been approved for a structure along the northern edge of the property at 720 25th Ave, near E Cherry.
Designed in partnership with Architects Without Borders – Seattle , the installation consists of three stacked panels of marine-grade plywood measuring roughly 12 feet wide by 8 feet tall.

The mural honors Eygi, a 26-year-old Seattle activist and UW psychology and Middle Eastern languages graduate who was killed in September 2024 by Israeli forces while demonstrating against settlement expansion in the West Bank. Prior to her death, Eygi had taken part in pro-Palestinian campus protests and negotiations at UW.

Designed by artist James Hesketh , the artwork depicts Eygi wearing a keffiyeh set against an olive tree, poppies, and tulips. More than 100 community members, friends, and family contributed to painting the panels paint-by-numbers style during a gathering at Cherry Street Village that marked what would have been her 28th birthday.
A segment representing Eygi was added to The Olympia-Rafah Solidarity Mural this fall (Image: @jameshesketh_ )

The Eygi mural project is being funded through donations and volunteer work and will add to the Central District’s collection of community murals including The People’s Wall at 19th and Spruce that received official city landmarks protections this summer.

Cherry Street Village is a social justice collective, community hub, and intentional living space co-directed by activist Samia El-Moslimany . Operating out of a property home to The Islamic School of Seattle into the 2010s, the village formed to host grassroots organizing, cultural events, mutual aid, and activist workshops. Today, it serves as a neighborhood gathering site for civil rights and solidarity efforts.

The new mural structure will stand one to two feet above the ground, supported by side posts and horizontal framing anchored into cast-in-place concrete piers. A small, cantilevered rooflet will sit atop the frame to shield the painted surface from Pacific Northwest weather.
Organizers have planned to unveil the permanent installation for neighborhood residents and passersby this fall.

articles.title: New superintendent, renewed closures: Capitol Hill’s Stevens Elementary proposed to merge into Montlake
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Families lined up against the closure in 2024

In a renewed push for campus consolidations amid declining districtwide enrollment, Seattle Public Schools has introduced a proposal to merge Capitol Hill’s Stevens Elementary into Montlake Elementary for the 2027–2028 school year,

“I don’t want students to spend one more year in a building where bookcases serve as walls, if we don’t have to,” Superintendent Ben Shuldiner wrote in a district newsletter this weekend as word of the renewed push spread.

“I don’t want students to spend one more year in a sixth-seventh-eighth grade split if we don’t have to. I don’t want teachers to be the only teacher in the grade if we don’t have to. I don’t want to accept large class sizes if we don’t have to. So, the conversation around school mergers begins.”

More accurately, the conversation re-starts. The announcement revives consolidation efforts that stalled two years ago. In late 2024, Seattle Public Schools backed away from a plan that would have shuttered up to 21 elementary campuses, including the Stevens campus along 19th Ave E at Galer just east of Volunteer Park .
Broad community resistance and pushback from families led district officials to back away from those closures .

Systemwide enrollment has now dropped from more than 94,000 students in 1964 to under 50,000 today. Shuldiner says that smaller campuses face operational challenges, including multi-grade split classrooms, solitary grade-level teachers, and limited access to full-time arts and music specialists.
There are major financial stakes to the consolidation plan.

Across the district, Seattle Public Schools has wrestled with annual deficits between $90 million and $130 million as enrollment fell below 50,000 students. In previous consolidation tries, the district estimated that shuttering an elementary campus generates roughly $750,000 to $1.5 million in annual operational savings by cutting administrative overhead, utility costs, and custodial services, while instructional staffing follows students to receiving sites.

Montlake Elementary was prepared for the changes following a nearly $80 million modernization and expansion completed in 2025. The rebuilt campus can accommodate up to 500 students, adding modern classrooms, an integrated library and cafeteria, and energy-efficient systems that replaced decades-old portable classrooms.

Beyond general elementary consolidations, Shuldiner said that the district is reviewing options for specialized programs across the city. This includes the Central District’s Seattle World School on E Union, which serves immigrant and refugee secondary students. Shuldiner said that the school itself will not be shuttered, but district leadership is exploring partnerships with one or more comprehensive high schools to strengthen its academic offerings.
The district is also evaluating site locations for its Bridges transition programs and Interagency Academy sites.

Aside from Stevens, no other neighborhood elementary schools in Capitol Hill or the Central District including Lowell, McGilvra, Leschi, Madrona, or Bailey Gatzert are being considered for closure in this round.
The changes will mean different patterns for families living in the area.

Under Seattle Public Schools student assignment rules, elementary students residing outside a one-mile “walk zone” qualify for bus transportation; however, for many families living in the Stevens area around 19th Ave E, Volunteer Park, and E Galer, the shift to Montlake’s campus at 2409 22nd Avenue E extends the commute up to 1.5 miles across a steep hill. Walking or biking routes will put more kids on busy arterials like Boyer and 24th and the Lake Washington Blvd corridor near 520. If the merger is finalized by the School Board in early 2027, the district’s transportation department will be required to run new walkshed hazard evaluations and adjust bus routing tiers.

Shuldiner took over as superintendent this year, buoyed in the role by the city’s newly approved $1.3 billion families and education levy that could provide funding for the Stevens campus to be part of expansion of programs including city-partnered early learning hubs, SPP preschool classrooms, or specialized programs like Bridges and Interagency..

In addition to the levy funding, transportation, walking, and biking concerns, Seattle City Hall may also have more to say about the proposed Stevens plan — of a more personal note. Mayor Katie Wilson has talked about living in the Stevens assignment area and her child is currently enrolled in the city-funded Seattle Preschool Program .

The new Stevens consolidation push is being rolled out for a more solid, perhaps better communicated process. The announcements come weeks before key meetings. Officials emphasized that no final decisions have been made on any site. In a joint message sent to their school communities, Stevens Principal Peter Donovan and Montlake Principal Tina Wood announced a family listening session planned for early December at Montlake Elementary.

“This work is currently in Phase 1, focused on listening, learning, and gathering feedback. No decisions have been made. Your voices, experiences, and perspectives are important as we begin these conversations,” Donovan and Wood wrote.
Under the district’s schedule, leadership and principal consultations continue through October, while meetings with school staff will run through the beginning of November.
Joint family conversations at proposed receiving sites follow throughout November and conclude in mid-December.

Once staff and family feedback is gathered, Shuldiner plans to formally present the consolidation recommendations to the Seattle School Board and the public around late December. That presentation will launch a 60-day window for public hearings and community forums in January and February, leading up to a final school board vote in late February or early March 2027.

To assist transitioning households, the district will give displaced students open enrollment transfer priority and will keep its school choice application window open until one week after the board’s final vote.

articles.title: Ninth Circuit hears Christian group’s challenge to Seattle permit rules over clash at 2025 Cal Anderson Park anti-trans event
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A three-judge panel of the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals was scheduled to hear oral arguments Monday in Johnson v. City of Seattle reviewing whether the city’s public event permitting system violates the First Amendment.

The lawsuit stems from the volatile May 24, 2025 demonstration at Cal Anderson Park in where organizers with Mayday USA were met by a spirited protest against the anti-trans “#DontMessWithOurKids” event. The Seattle Police Department crackdown on protesters resulted in strong backlash against the department and Mayor Bruce Harrell and months of investigations including the recent “written reprimand” of a lieutenant over his “here to fuck people up” commands captured on body-worn video as SPD prepared to move in on demonstrators against an anti-trans Christian group’s rally.

In the court action, lawyers for Christian revival organizers are appealing a Western District of Washington decision that denied their motion for a preliminary injunction against Seattle officials after the city denied organizers a permit for a worship event downtown and rerouted them to Cal Anderson Park where the conflict with demonstrators and police played out.
In their filings, plaintiffs contend Seattle enforces an unconstitutional prior restraint that grants officials unchecked discretion to restrict speech based on viewpoint and public reaction.
“The result was exactly what you might expect: violent attacks on the Christians,” the plaintiff’s brief reads.
Seattle is defending its permitting scheme as content-neutral, arguing plaintiffs lack standing to seek prospective injunctive relief.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 26–November 1
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Shannon Lubetich, Megan Seling, and Audrey Vann
paras: (MUSIC) Wanna feel old? It’s been 10 years since Greta Kline, aka Frankie Cosmos, released her 2016 studio album Next Thing , which contains some of her most well-known songs, including “Fool,” “Sappho,” and “Outside With the Cuties.” The dreamy, wistful record features influences from poet Frank O’Hara and musician Arthur Russell, with Kline’s floaty vocals and contemplative lyrics layered over soft synths. It packs the emotional punch of a coming-of-age film into the span of 28 minutes and 28 seconds and defined my 20s—in fact, I am having an existential spiral realizing that it’s been a decade since I attended the Vera Project show for Frankie Cosmos’s West Coast tour promoting this album alongside former Seattle favorites iji (now based in Los Angeles). Kline and her band will return to Seattle to celebrate Next Thing ’s anniversary at the Crocodile, with an opening set by hometown heroes Coral Grief, and I fully expect it to heal me. ( Crocodile, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) I’ve been a fan of Dolly Parton’s spiritual successor Kacey Musgraves since her 2013 single “Follow Your Arrow,” and it’s been a treat to watch her career evolve over the years. Her bittersweet latest album, Middle of Nowhere , finds her deep in her single era, evoking both liminal spaces and her Texan roots—the title comes from a sign she spotted in her hometown that read, “​​Golden, Texas: Somewhere in the middle of nowhere.” It’s by turns horny, as on the touch-starved bop “Dry Spell” (“Ain’t nobody’s tool up in my shed / Ain’t nobody’s boots under my bed”), and heartbreaking, as on the ballad “Hell on Me.” She also works out a 15-year feud with country star Miranda Lambert on the remix in their duet “Horses and Divorces”: “It’s all whiskey under the bridge.” Seattle-based sibling busker trio the Brudi Brothers will kick off Musgraves’s show at Climate Pledge Arena. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(PERFORMANCE) The Seattle Opera is kicking off the season with Richard Strauss’s single-act opera Salome , adapted to German from Oscar Wilde’s play, which was originally written in French. Strauss’s take on the play famously strips down Wilde’s original story, removing Wilde’s motifs and leaving its most thrilling and shocking elements. What remains is an hour-and-a-half tragedy (which is actually short by opera standards). The piece shocked audiences when it premiered back in 1905 because of its Biblical nature blended with erotic and murderous elements. Don’t miss the Seattle Opera’s production, which will be brought to life through stunning sets from Leslie Travers, 80-plus members of the Seattle Symphony, and Grammy-nominated soprano Brenda Rae. ( McCaw Hall, 7:30 pm ) AUDREY VANN

(MUSIC) I’m hard-pressed to think of many artists who reinvent themselves as effortlessly and confidently as Beatrice Laus, better known by her stage name beabadoobee. The Filipino British singer-songwriter rose to fame with her debut single, “Coffee,” which went viral on YouTube in 2017 and blew up even more after it was sampled on Canadian rapper ​​Powfu’s TikTok-popular 2019 song “Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head).” Two years after her indie-pop album This Is How Tomorrow Moves , she’s adopting an edgier, grungier sound with her new album Pylon , which incorporates ’90s alt influences and enlists Hayley Williams, Pinegrove’s Evan Stephens Hall, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates as collaborators. Laus’s ethereal vocals recall the Cranberries’ Dolores O’Riordan over fuzzy, shoegaze-tinged guitars, simmering with heartbreak and nostalgia—the album gets its title from the pylon towers she’d gaze at out the window while homesick on tour. Up-and-coming nu-gaze artist Wisp will join her on her first arena tour. ( Climate Pledge, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Rebecca Black has successfully shed the skin of her notoriously cringe viral bop “Friday.” Today, her public persona leans into her status as a queer icon, hyperpop sensation, and collaborator of genre rule-breakers like Dylan Brady (100 gecs), Big Freedia, and Dorian Electra. On her sophomore album, Age of the Exhibitionist , she harmonizes about kink and pleasure à la Madonna’s Erotica . Explaining to Out Magazine her hopes for the album, Black said, “I hope [listeners] sweat, I hope they fuck, I hope they do everything they need to do. There really is a song for everything on this record.” Brooklyn-based artist BAYLI will open with her signature blend of club, rap, and pop bangers. ( Showbox, 7 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

(PARTY) Break out your black eyeliner and pleather pants; it’s time for Southgate Roller Rink’s Goth Skate and Halloween party. You can bring your own skates or grab rentals to join goblins, ghouls, fairies, princesses, and other costumed characters out on the rink while DJs, bands, drag artists, and go-gos perform on two different stages. The live music lineup is stacked with Heebie Jeebies’ surf-punk takes of Halloween classics, the Holy Divers of Babylon’s heavy metal tribute, the Band That Ate My Brain’s punk covers, Ghosts in the Graveyard’s theatrical deathrock, and Neuroprison’s post-punk darkwave tunes. If thrills are what you seek, head out to the beer garden for a hair-raising haunted house. ( Southgate Roller Rink, 9 pm, 21+ ) SHANNON LUBETICH

(FOOD) Sure, it’s confusing that Seattle Restaurant Week is actually two weeks, but that just means we have twice as much time to pig out on specials from dozens of delicious participating restaurants. And there are some true superstars on the list. Lupe’s Situ Tacos in Ballard will be offering a few different specials, including three of their incredibly crispy tacos, or five taquitos, served alongside a cup of soup, aguas frescas, and baklava for $30. That’s enough food for two! (Though I do hate to share my taquitos.) There’s also Shiro’s Sushi, Marination in Columbia City (and, hell yeah, their special includes malasadas), Kilig, which Stranger contributor Meg van Huygen put on her 2024 Best Restaurants in the Seattle Area list, and Melting Pot in Bellevue. I did not know Melting Pot still existed! The ’90s really are back. (Various locations) MEGAN SELING

articles.title: Slog AM: Less Rain in Seattle Than LA, Brazil Rejects Far-Right in Election, Snohomish Mama Bear on the Run
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Seattle just got some rain, breaking an odd drought. We’ve been getting less rain than Los Angeles and Las Vegas, Nevada. These are the first fingerprints of El Niño, which disrupts moisture and temperature patterns around the Pacific, the Emerald City Weather Blog ’s Scott Sistek reports.

Wrong kind of woke: A shootout involving five different firearms emptying at least 80 rounds woke up a sleeping woman at her home off Aurora, KIRO reports. The woman told reporters the gunfire jolted her out of and then under her bed on Saturday morning. A bullet hole landed above her bed. “It was the scariest moment of my life,” Hannah, who used only her first name, told the station.

Give me a “U”! The NFL has its first cheerleaders union, NBC reports . According to WFFA , the Dallas Cowboys voluntarily recognized the freshly formed Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association, clearing the way for a collective bargaining agreement. The squad’s three dozen cheerleaders have at times made less than minimum wage, but won pay increases thanks to a Netflix documentary. Hopefully the dominoes will begin to fall on unpaid and underpaid entertaining across professional sports.

Five new murals are finished around Capitol Hill. The murals created by On the Block and the Seattle Artist Coalition for Equitable Development are supported by city funding , Capitol Hill Seattle reports . Backers of the project are also arguing that $8 million of the Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed $556 million police budget should be diverted to artists.

BRAZIL ELECTION YESTERDAY: WORKERS PARTY BEAT ULTRA-RIGHT, AGAIN. Geriatric union leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat authoritarian nepo baby Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s election by a solid 10 million votes, Folha de S.Paulo reports. There are many , many , many takes as to what happened and what it means for the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest country and the guardian of the world’s oxygen factory.

As I posted on BlueSky last night, Lula’s victory is good for the Amazon, good for public health, and good for secularism in a country of 220 million people. Like his coup-attempting dad, Flávio is a Trumpian, corrupt , election-denying mess . Donald Trump Jr. is already complaining about the election results, so look for hot takes on MAGA TikTok. Lula has now hit his term limit, giving the Brazilian left four years to find a proper replacement.
🗺️ Reddit made a map of how Brazil’s election would have gone if it had an electoral college like the U. instead of the popular vote. Yes, R/MAPPORN is the best.

ISRAEL ELECTION TOMORROW: A BATTLE OF MID VS EVIL. Israel will decide between center-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot or ultra-right Benjamin Netanyahu, shunned for his complicity in a predecessor’s assasination , wanted for alleged genocide against Gazans , and lampooned for failing to prevent the Oct. 7 massacre by Hamas despite multiple warnings. Netanyahu, who came to power thanks to the death of his war hero brother, is so desperate to win— and stay out of jail —that he has pleaded on the phone with Trump twice in 3 days, Axios reports , earning him another Truth Social post. Eisenkot opposes a Palestinian state, but supports an impartial investigation into leaders (including himself) who failed to prevent Oct. 7. He also supports cracking down on Israeli settler violence.

Snohomish woman seriously injured by mother bear. The woman apparently found herself near the mama bear’s cub while trying to take out her trash, KING 5 reports . Reports of her injuries varied over the weekend but involved her being clawed, knocked over, and possibly bitten . Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife officials failed in their initial attempts to locate and trap the mother bear. WDFW wouldn’t rule out executing the bear telling KING 5 that “decisions to lethally remove wildlife are never easy and many factors are taken into consideration when determining next steps.” I am rooting for the injured woman’s speedy and full recovery, and the Wanted Mama Bear’s clean escape into Mount Pilchuck.

Another DNA clue leads to murder charges in a cold case: Spokane police found the suspect in the 1986 murder of Mary Ann Turner by matching semen and other DNA from under her fingernails to a family genealogy database, t he Spokesman-Review reports .
The West Seattle Blog did a nice profile of their tool lending library. Tool lending libraries are awesome. If you’re not sure where the nearest one is, King County has a list .

AMERICAN ELECTIONS IN 8 DAYS : If you are missing your ballot, or your cat ate it, you can get a replacement ballot at votewa.gov or go to any county election office . There’s still time to register to vote online ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election.

PNW takes center stage in MAGA’s election interference. The Department of Justice filed a baseless lawsuit in Alaska that would seek to interfere with the state’s election certification only if the Republican incumbent loses. The DOJ is currently run by Trump’s personal lawyer. Trump said he directed the DOJ to file the suit. “President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche told CNN, according to NPR .

The lawsuit argues that voters will be confused about two similar names on the ballot: “Dan S. Sullivan” and “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” Two problems with the lawsuit: First, Voters are unlikely to be confused—Dan S is marked on the ballot as a registered Republican and the incumbent. Even Alaska’s Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski—who is endorsing Dan S. —says the suit should not have been filed . Second,there’s no federal law giving the White House a say. The DOJ’s lawsuit is so off base legal experts are calling it an embarrassment, CNN reports .

Campaign finance laws are apparently useless in WA. Washington state’s campaign finance watchdog, the Public Disclosure Commission (PDC), won’t try to enforce a $75,000 cap on issue contributions, the Seattle Times reports . Speaking out of both sides of the mouth , the PDC said that it can’t determine the constitutionality of the law, but has directed staff to not enforce it. Political action committee leaders from the right and left denounced the move, which could affect races for the state Supreme Court and the shitty statewide ballot initiatives . The only real winners in the PDC’s decision appear to be the rich.

Protesters took to a SeaTac parking lot to speak out against ICE and Palantir . Protesters rallied Sunday calling for Seattle-Tacoma International Airport to cut ties with Palantir, Fox 13 reported . The protest was a lot more tame than the civil disobedience that happened two years ago protesting the genocide in Gaza.

Who controls US foreign policy? Elon Musk admitted he throttled the Ukrainian military’s Starlink internet service, disrupting capabilities it relies on to defend against Russia, t he Associated Press Reports . The acknowledgement oozed out after a long blame game between the Pentagon, the White House, and Starbase. Even conservative pundit Ramesh Ponnuru, editor of the National Review, saw through this bullshit.

articles.title: In the CID, Stories Fill the Eng Family Home
paras: What does a house contain in addition to its residents and their belongings? The Eng Family Home , nestled between loquat trees and small businesses in the Chinatown-International District (CID), holds many stories of a Chinese American family who, after living in an apartment in the neighborhood's Canton Alley, built this one-story, single-family residence just a couple of blocks away.

Wing Luke Museum acquired the Eng Family Home in 2021 for $1.8 million to preserve it and to incorporate the home as an immersive exhibit, representing the experience of one family in the CID during the early 20th century. The home will be open for guided public tours starting Oct. 29. A $30 admission includes access to the museum.

The home was built by Suen King Eng, who founded and managed Min Hing Knitting Company for the Eng Corporation. His wife, Sue Fong, ran a bean sprout business out of the home's basement. The family added Eng's Grocery, Golden Star Cafe, and King's Chinese Hand Laundry to the list of family businesses as they provided for their family in Seattle and sent money to relatives in Guangdong, China, during the Great Depression.

"If [the Eng] family's future generations can't live in the house and maintain it, the next best thing is for it to be in the Wing's hands, to tell not only our story, but all people who came to Seattle and were othered," said Sue May Eng, the granddaughter of Suen King and Sue Fong, referring to discriminatory practices like redlining. Communities of color were segregated from white communities, and exclusionary laws blocked Chinese women from immigrating to the U.S. until the mid-1900s.

Side x Side Architects and Metis Construction restored portions of the space and retrofitted it for ADA accessibility and a new staircase. Wing Luke Museum worked with the family to create the exhibit. The museum purchased items and gathered items from the family, its own collections, and the community to create a space that reflects the historical period of the home.

This is not the first time the museum has purchased land in the neighborhood. The museum is in the East Kong Yick building, built with money pooled by more than 150 Chinese immigrants in 1910. It acquired the building in 2003 for $2 million. "Many Chinatowns, Japantowns, and Manilatowns have been lost over the years," said Wing Luke Museum board member Diane Narasaki. "The Wing is preserving community by purchasing property that has historic significance. It keeps property owned by a community-based organization, so it doesn't get sold to an outside developer who may not have particular interest in the community."
Before the space opens to visitors, Sue May and her father, Tuck Ling Eng (Suen King and Sue Fong's son), sat down with the Emerald . Here's what they had to say about their family.
Tuck's parents (center photo) and grandparents are featured on the living room wall.

Because of Chinese exclusion laws that lasted into the mid-20th century, Chinatowns throughout North America were communities of men who worked and sent money to relatives in China. At that time, women from China were often barred entry into the U.S. This reality impacted the Eng family experience in Seattle.

Tuck says his paternal grandfather (pictured at far left in a Western-style suit) arrived in the city in the late 1800s and established Eng Trading Company with a relative. His maternal grandfather went to work in Vancouver, Canada.
Tuck said the grandmothers "never made it here."

In 1921, Tuck's paternal grandfather brought Tuck's father, Suen King, to the U.S. Suen King had a wife and children still living in China. Though exclusionary laws made immigration for Chinese women less accessible, Suen King was able to bring his wife, Sue Fong, and a daughter to Seattle in 1927. The mother and daughter were incarcerated at the Immigration and Naturalization Service for six months before they were released. The eldest daughter arrived from Guangdong in 1949.
Along with Sue Fong giving birth to children in China, she also gave birth to children in the U.S. Tuck, the youngest child in the family, was born in 1933.

In 1937, Suen King acquired land for a house through a contractor. Because non-U.S. citizens couldn't own property in Seattle, the site was deeded to Suen King's 8-year-old son, William, who had birthright citizenship.

Suen King planned a two-story, three-bedroom frame house with a full basement. "The City approved the permit at first," said Tuck. "Then, after the foundation was poured, they issued a stop-order of the construction, saying that frame houses weren't allowed on that side of 8th Avenue South due to a zoning change."

Despite the limitations, Suen King built a one-story, three-bedroom home with a half-basement per permit requirements. Since a frame house was not permitted, he had a choice of bricks or cinder blocks. Suen King went with cinder blocks manufactured just a few blocks away.
Suen King and Sue Fong had six children and 17 grandchildren, which meant a group of nearly 30 people gathered in the roughly 1,800-square-foot house each Sunday for dinner.
"Back then, there was a whole backyard there with a fig tree, a sandbox, greenhouse, chicken coops, and a fish pond," Sue May said.

Sue May says that after school and during the summer, cousins were dropped off in the morning when the parents went to work, and these grandchildren stayed at the house until they were picked up in the evening or after dinner.

"The first thing I learned in Toisanese was 'hoy mon,' which meant 'open the door,' because when we get to the front door, there's a mail slot, and we would push [the flap] and say, 'Hoy mon, hoy mon, hoy mon,'" said Sue May.
Her father, Tuck, chuckled. "[Pushing the flap in and letting go] sounded like 'bang, bang, bang,'" he said.

During the Great Depression, the family struggled financially to raise six children along with sending money to relatives in Guangdong. Tuck said that at the time, his father made $48 a month. "Before my dad would go to work, Dad and Mom would go out to pick watercress, purslane, seaweed, or cabbage sprouts early in the morning in places like Auburn, Kent, Richmond Beach, and Tacoma," said Tuck. His mother would sell them to local restaurants, and, Tuck said, "If she sold 100 of them for 10 cents a bundle, she could make a lot more money than my father could in a month."
Later, Sue Fong learned how to cultivate bean sprouts from elders at the Wah Sang Co. grocery store.

Daryl Eng, a grandson of Suen King and Sue Fong, remembered piling the mung bean sacks to the ceiling in the basement with another cousin. At the time, he was about 8. "We sterilized the equipment, bleached them, washed the mung beans, watered them three times a day, and drained them. Then, we'd hull all of the sprouts using water. When they were long enough, we needed to pull them out of the containers without breaking the sprouts, or they go bad quickly," said Daryl.

Sue May recounted taking bean sprout orders to restaurants. "We liked to go to Gim Ling [restaurant], through the alley to the back door, and you'd go downstairs, and you give them their bean sprouts. They would give us all chicken wings. We loved it."

Suen King established Min Hing Knitting Co. in 1932 and managed it for the Eng Corporation after learning how to produce knitted fabric. The store, located near Hing Hay Park, also sold men's furnishings. Min Hing Knitting Co. closed in the late 1940s.

Suen King opened other businesses, including King's Chinese Hand Laundry in the mid-1940s, where Tuck and his siblings ironed handkerchiefs, darned socks, and starched collars and cuffs. "We were known for premium white shirts," said Tuck. "Undertakers and attorneys came for their white shirts. We would send out the clothes for a wet wash on Friday. On Sunday, we'd hang up the wet clothes in a drying room and build a fire to warm them. Then we'd go out for 'Sunday Fun Day.'"
There were other Eng family shops, including the Golden Star Cafe, which operated from 1944 into the early 1950s, and Eng's Grocery Store, which ran from 1964 until the late 1960s.

"Living in the house as a kid, we had to keep the house clean. We had to cook dinner. We hulled the bean sprouts and spread them in the backyard for compost. We had dinner at six and studied from eight to midnight," said Tuck. "Sunday was our relax day. Dad would take us to Triple X and treat us to hamburgers."

"Mom would go into the mountains and harvest herbs," said Tuck. "She'd buy other herbs at the store. She'd make alcohol from a rice-potato mash in a still. Then she'd make tinctures that would sit for a year before she'd dispense them. She would make formulas. One was Het Ah Diu in Toisanese, which was good for bruises. She would give this formula away. She never charged for that medicine. I still have a batch of that made by her."

As a group, people aged 18 to 24 vote at rates lower than other age groups. According to policy research group KFF, about 28% of Washington residents aged 18 to 24 voted in the 2022 general election, compared with 78% of Washington residents aged 65 and older.
In addition to El Centro de la Raza, other groups represented at the get out the vote events included League of Women Voters and King County Elections.
El Centro de la Raza also brought local social media influencers, like Lorena Soriano, who runs momchangetheworld on Instagram , to spread the word.

“I feel like we're all just kind of getting excited where it's: we know that we can create change. Our voice matters.” Soriano said. “Either we're first gens or we're zero gens or like second generation. I'm a Latina. I'm a Mexicana. We have not always had a seat at the table. We have not always had the right. And now that we do have this right, let's use our power, our poder. And just, like El Centro says, juntos creamos cambio.”
John Cortes who goes by Corteezyy on TikTok and Instagram says he wants to change people’s skepticism of voting.

“The world doesn't look like voting is what matters right now. ‘My bills are too high. My gas is crazy. I can't even afford groceries. So, like, why do I need to focus on voting?’ And so like, rightfully so. I agree with all that. But the reason why these things are so high is because of voting,” he said.

“In a world right now where it doesn't look the best. I promise you, we can make a difference. We can. We can definitely change the trajectory of, like, what things are looking like right now and don't lose hope,” Cortes said.
“I wish that someone had taught me about these things.. when I was young,” he added. “I'm trying to fill that role.”

articles.title: Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana Timmerman
articles.author: Jordana Timerman
paras: After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment

The impossible happened. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in Sunday’s runoff election in Brazil, overturning Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in a historic comeback. No candidate has ever lost the first round and won the second, until now. Grassroots mobilisation, alongside social welfare policies, helped turn the contest into a referendum on Brazilian democracy, rallying voters against a candidate seeking to restore the legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, imprisoned for plotting a coup after his 2022 defeat. Lula’s victory suggests that defending democracy can still be a powerful electoral argument against the ascendant right.

Having already consolidated most of the leftwing vote, Lula had limited room to attract supporters of other candidates after his first-round defeat. His best chance lay in mobilising abstainers and reconnecting with working-class voters. The Workers’ party intensified its grassroots and digital campaigns, using social media influencers and messaging networks to reach supporters. Nearly 3 million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, and Lula gained ground across the country, particularly in major cities and his north-eastern strongholds. He also appealed to voters’ immediate economic concerns, drawing on a record of reducing poverty and inequality, and increasing benefits under Bolsa Família , the landmark welfare programme he launched in 2003. Lula framed the election as a choice between protecting social gains and democratic institutions, or returning to the Bolsonaro family’s attacks on both, warning that his opponent would compromise Brazil’s sovereignty by aligning himself with Donald Trump.
Jordana Timerman is a journalist based in Buenos Aires. She is the managing editor of The Ideas Letter and compiles the Latin America Daily Briefing

articles.title: Sin or virtue? How envy can actually be helpful
articles.author: Adrienne Matei
paras: In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals

In the 16th-century poem The Faerie Queene, envy is a ghoulish figure riding a ravenous wolf, sad to see the fortune of others and “wonderous glad” of their hardship. It’s not a flattering depiction; better to be thankful for what we have, rather than dwell on such a bitter and self-destructive feeling, right?

Maybe not. “I think that when we don’t examine our envy, that’s when it leads us astray,” says Dr Stacy Kim, social scientist, life coach and author of the new book Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want. Kim wrote the book after seeing the way envy came up for her coaching clients and reflecting on the role it had in her own life. The book is informed by social science and philosophy research, as well as her personal and professional experiences.
Similar target: “You remind yourself: ‘Hey, the reason why I’m feeling this envy is because what I want is within my reach,’” she says.
Relevant comparison: Identify which specific domain – something you care about or already participate in – is relevant to your desires
Negative emotion: How long does it last? How intense is the message it’s sending? This tells us how important the feeling is.
Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want by Stacy S Kim is out now via Balance

articles.title: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America
articles.author: Jesse Hassenger in New York
paras: Nathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to think
In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain
Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year

When I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything a second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers.

This documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite an Obsession -level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hit Primetime , which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.
