articles.title: Ghost stories don’t just scare us – they remind us of historical injustices
articles.author:
<name>Marcus Librizzi, Professor of English, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/marcus-librizzi-2767527"/>
paras: Along with the pumpkins and costumes, the candles and cobwebs, Halloween is all about storytelling. From tales of haunted houses to accounts of demonic possession, ghost stories are part of the holiday’s appeal.

As a professor at the University of Maine who specializes in ghost stories, I’ve thought a lot about what makes one unforgettable. My field research has taken me from the coast of Maine to the Amazon jungle, but some factors remain constant in an unforgettable tale.
One factor is what I call “creep value,” which includes the scare factor but also the elements of a story that might be simply unsettling or uncanny.

Take, for starters, the ghost of Catherine’s Hill along the Blacks Woods Road in Maine. The story warns that, against all intuition, even a lone driver at night must always stop and offer the phantom woman a ride . If not, as the story goes, she will appear when least expected in the back seat of the car to cause a fatal accident.

But there is more to account for than creep value in an unforgettable ghost story. These stories can keep alive the memory of a dark past. In my research I have come across tales that preserve memories of injustices that might otherwise have been forgotten.
One story, about a ghost ship that can be heard but never seen, preserves the little-known history of the smuggling of enslaved people.

The legend goes that on foggy nights, during the full moon, those standing at the Cooksey Drive Overlook in Seal Harbor, just outside Acadia National Park, can hear the slaves in the hold of a sinking ship crying for help.

The story goes back to the Pride of the Seas , a ship that smuggled enslaved Africans into the United States after the trans-Atlantic slave trade had been abolished but slavery remained legal. The account specifies that the smugglers scuttled the ship to evade the law. In ghost stories that circulate by word of mouth on Mount Desert Island, the screams of those left behind can still be heard.

Pennsylvania coal miners offer another example of past grievances passed down in the form of ghost stories. At the sites of deadly accidents, people have reported the sound of a pickaxe or the groans of a dying man. An extensive archive contains multiple accounts of coal miners witnessing ghostly knocking, disembodied voices and apparitions of mangled men. One story involves an innocent coal miner, condemned to death in 1877, who left a handprint in his cell at the Carbon County Jail that no amount of sanding or paint has been able to erase.

Today, it is widely known that coal miners of the 19th and early 20th centuries experienced ruthless exploitation and hazardous working conditions. Years ago, their plight went unrecognized in official histories and government policies, but ghost stories helped keep these experiences in the collective memory.
When I collected ghost stories in South America, the same pattern held true: Some tales preserved history that would otherwise be lost.

In the Amazon jungle of northern Brazil, I traveled to a gloomy site where people, over several generations, have claimed to see the spirits of young men in the murky water. These stories keep alive injustices from the 19th century involving enslavement of Indigenous people . The location was a former sugarcane plantation notorious for cruelty, and accounts of apparitions in the water are a reminder of this history.

In Rio de Janeiro a well-known ghost story involves the apparition of a young girl in a mansion known as the Castelinho do Flamengo . All the accounts of her story agree that this young heiress, named Maria de Lourdes Fernandes, witnessed the deaths of her parents; her guardian then locked her up and drove her to suicide to get her inheritance.

Her soul is said to remain in the mansion she tried to escape. The tale is not just about an individual tragedy but one that exposes inequities involving the mistreatment of juveniles and the corrupting influence of power.
Ghost stories don’t simply recount memories – they can revive them and bring the past back into the present.
The unsolved 1898 murder of a 52-year-old woman, Sarah Ware, in Bucksport, Maine, illustrates how ghost stories can have historical significance and flood the present with the past.

In the 1980s a woman and her daughter began having nightmares about a long-haired woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of a lake. When they realized they were having the same recurring dream , they partnered with an author, and their research led them to a conclusion that the apparition was the ghost of Ware.

Official records document that when Ware’s body was recovered it was badly decomposed and her head had completely detached . Her head remained in the courthouse until the 1990s, when it was buried in Ware’s grave. According to local lore, however, Ware’s headless body is not in that grave but instead in her original grave, now located at the bottom of Silver Lake. In the oral history of the area, workers moved only the tombstones when they flooded the paupers’ graveyard – the cemetery for the poor – to make a reservoir in the 1930s.

Ware’s ghost is believed to have appeared again in 2006. When a young woman went scuba diving in Silver Lake in Bucksport, she reported seeing a woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of the lake. When she swam over to help, the figure’s hair floated back with the movement of the water to reveal she was a faceless apparition. The sighting of the faceless ghost revived the history of the unsolved murder all over again.

Ware’s case highlights the violence and injustice and their connection to gender and social class in 19th-century Maine. Missing evidence and recanted testimonies suggest that powerful men might have interfered with the investigation to hide their own complicity in the murder. As an independent woman of the time, Ware was the subject of gossip, and the treatment of her body shows how social class affects even the honoring of the dead. As a ghost story, the history of Sarah Ware is not past but rather part of the here and now.

So when you’re out and about telling ghost stories this Halloween, remember that the unforgettable ones are all about creep value in the context of a dark history that flows back in again like the tide.
Marcus Librizzi previously received funding from the Maine Humanities Council.

articles.title: If Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts can get dangerous blood clots, so can you – here’s how some states are trying to reduce the risk
articles.author:
<name>Ali Ataya, Professor of Medicine, University of Florida</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ali-ataya-2772902"/>
paras: Jalen Hurts is 28, a Super Bowl MVP and an elite athlete in peak physical condition. He was also recently diagnosed with blood clots in his leg and both lungs .

After a cleat to the left calf during a game against the Los Angeles Rams on Oct. 4, 2026, and after a team flight to London, the Philadelphia Eagles quarterback was given an ultrasound and diagnosed with a superficial vein thrombosis, which is a blood clot in the vein near the skin, in his left leg.
He played that Sunday. A follow-up ultrasound showed the superficial vein clot had progressed to a deeper vein, and he was diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis, or DVT.

By Oct. 19, he was diagnosed with a bilateral pulmonary embolism, which means he had blood clots in both lungs. He started treatment with blood thinners, and his prognosis was described as “very good,” according to a statement from the team and his agent , but he will likely be out for the rest of the season .

For me, as a pulmonary vascular disease specialist who treats patients with blood clots and pulmonary embolisms, this case highlights an important teaching moment. If this can happen to an elite athlete, it can happen to anyone. And too often, it can be prevented.
Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are grouped under one name: venous thromboembolism .

When a deep vein thrombosis develops, the clot can break off and a piece of it can travel through the body and lodge in the arteries in the lungs, where it obstructs blood flow and lowers oxygen in the blood, causing shortness of breath and strain on the heart. This is known as pulmonary embolism . If the blood clot in the lungs is large enough, it can sometimes kill within hours.

Clots that happen near the skin, like the one first found in Hurts’ leg, are often treated as minor but are not always harmless. It is estimated that a quarter of people diagnosed with superficial clots can also have deep vein thrombosis, so health providers order follow-up imaging.

In the United States, up to 900,000 people are affected by venous thromboembolism each year. An estimated 60,000 to 100,000 die from it annually. Survivors often have long-term symptoms such as persistent leg swelling, shortness of breath, chronic clots, or elevated blood pressure in the arteries in the lungs, which is known as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension .

The three main factors that drive formation of blood clots are injury to the vein wall, slow or stagnant blood flow in that injured region, and blood that clots easily due to inflammation or other factors. This is called Virchow’s triad, and Hurts’ story touches every corner of this triad.

The injury to the left calf bruised the muscle and likely the vein beneath it. Later, prolonged sitting on an overnight flight from Philadelphia to London and a return flight after the game resulted in stagnant blood flow to the injured leg. Inflammation from the injury along with dehydration from the game and jet lag all may have contributed to increased blood clotting.
Beyond Hurts’ case, the most common risk factors to developing venous thromboembolism include hospitalization and surgery, especially orthopedic surgery and abdominal operations.

More than a third of cases occur following a hospital admission or just after discharge. Fractures and blunt trauma to the legs, prolonged immobility or bed rest, having a leg in a cast, or sitting for hours in a plane or car all predispose to blood clot formation in the legs. The use of estrogen in birth control pills or hormone therapy, cancer, pregnancy and inherited clotting disorders also predispose an otherwise healthy person to develop blood clots.

It is estimated that up to 70% of hospital-associated clots can be avoided with prophylactic blood thinners or inflatable leg devices called sequential compression devices to prevent deep vein thrombosis. However, fewer than half of hospital patients receive such measures, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

For people taking long trips in a car or plane, it is recommended to take frequent movement breaks, stay hydrated and even use compression socks. New symptoms of calf swelling, tenderness or redness should raise concerns for possible deep vein thrombosis.
Hurts had elite doctors and close monitoring, so his clots were caught and treated quickly. Most individuals do not have the same protections.

In 2025, Florida was the first state in the country to pass a law to help identify and treat those at risk of blood clots. It’s called the Emily Adkins Family Protection Act . Adkins tragically passed away in 2022 at age 23 from a fatal pulmonary embolism that occurred after a clot from her leg traveled to her lungs. Her family helped pass the bill that set up the nation’s first state blood clot and pulmonary embolism work group , which put forward the recommendations that later turned into law.

Florida’s law requires hospitals to have protocols to assess and treat patients at risk of blood clots and train hospital staff to recognize the symptoms of venous thromboembolism. It also will involve the creation of a statewide venous thromboembolism registry, the first of its kind in the country, where hospitals will report data on blood clots.

Florida is no longer alone. In 2026, the Blake Burgess Blood Clot Prevention Act was passed in Oklahoma; Mississippi proposed similar legislation. Advocates such as the National Blood Clot Alliance are urging other states to follow .

Hurts will most likely recover over the next few months. The outcome for many other individuals will depend on whether someone asks the right questions, recognizes the warning signs and acts in time. Venous thromboembolism is one of the few major killers where risk assessment, prevention, early diagnosis and fast treatment can play a critical role in changing the outcome.

articles.title: Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
Why are people still getting polio in some countries and in not others? – Mia, age 9, Centennial, Colorado

On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a healthcare worker kneels down so she’s eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child’s tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child’s pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio.
During big vaccination drives, thousands of health workers like her knock on doors across Pakistan.
Most kids in the United States will never experience anything like this, because they get the polio vaccine as a shot at the doctor’s office instead of drops in a door-to-door campaign.

The two vaccines work a little differently , but both protect kids from the polio virus. The countries that still see polio outbreaks are places where not enough people have gotten the preventive vaccine.

I’m an epidemiologist – a scientist who studies how diseases spread. My work focuses on diseases that vaccines can prevent, and on the false information that keeps some families from getting those vaccines.

Polio is caused by a virus that lives in the human gut. It spreads when tiny bits of poop from an infected person get onto hands, food or water, and then into someone else’s mouth. That’s why polio spreads fastest in places without clean water or good sewer systems.
Polio is sneaky. Most people who catch it never feel sick at all , so they can pass it on without knowing.
But in about 1 out of every 200 infections globally, the virus attacks the nerves that control muscles, usually in the legs. This can cause a person to be paralyzed for the rest of their life.
There is no cure for polio. But there is a vaccine , and a few doses can protect you for life.
In 1988, polio paralyzed about 350,000 children in 125 countries. That same year, countries around the world teamed up with one huge goal: Wipe out polio for good.
Though polio has not yet been entirely eliminated, this effort has been a major success. Since then, polio cases have dropped by more than 99% globally .
There used to be three types of wild polio virus . Now, only type 1 is left.
Wild polio, the original virus, now spreads in just two countries : Afghanistan and Pakistan. In 2025, wild polio paralyzed 52 children there.
Both countries have lived through decades of war . In some areas, it’s too dangerous for vaccinators to travel, and some have even been attacked .

In Afghanistan, vaccinators haven’t gone house to house since late 2024 . Families must bring children to central spots, such as mosques, instead. But the kids who can’t get there miss their vaccines.
Some countries have outbreaks of a different kind, called vaccine-derived polio .

The oral polio vaccine, which is no longer used in many countries, including the U.S., contains a weakened polio virus – too weak to make a child sick, but strong enough to teach the body to fight polio.
After a child swallows the drops of vaccine, some of the weakened virus leaves their body in their poop. If nearly every kid around is vaccinated, the virus has nowhere to go and fizzles out.

But in areas where fewer than 80% of kids are vaccinated, it can pass from child to child. Like a message in a game of telephone, the virus changes a little each time it’s passed. Eventually, it can change back into a form that paralyzes children.
That might sound like the vaccine is the problem. But in fact, the problem is that too few kids have received the vaccine.

The children who go unvaccinated are usually the hardest to reach: kids in the poorest families, in faraway villages or in war zones. In one study in Pakistan, offering families other free healthcare along with polio drops cuts the share of never-vaccinated kids nearly in half .
In October 2025, scientists testing sewage in Hamburg, Germany, found wild polio . Its genes matched virus found in Afghanistan, more than 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away.
This means that someone carrying the virus, probably without feeling sick, had traveled to Germany. But not a single child there was paralyzed because most German kids are vaccinated against polio.
Other countries in Europe found vaccine-derived polio in their sewage in 2025, with the same happy ending.
Polio can travel anywhere, but it can only hurt kids where they aren’t protected by the vaccine.

Polio also gets help spreading from rumors and misinformation. In 2003, false stories that the vaccine was harmful led parts of northern Nigeria to stop vaccinating for almost a year . This led to a small outbreak that spread from that area to other countries.
Research shows that false news online travels “ farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than the truth.”

Unfortunately, misinformation could also contribute to a resurgence of polio in places where it has been eliminated – even the U.S. In Colorado , about 1 in 8 kindergartners haven’t had all their polio shots . And in 2022, vaccine-derived polio paralyzed an unvaccinated young man in New York.
Though rumors can travel quickly, trust is built one conversation at a time , by neighbors, religious leaders and doctors who take parents’ questions and concerns seriously.

Unfortunately, the budget of the worldwide program to end polio decreased by 30% in 2026, mostly because wealthy countries cut their foreign aid. This cut is largely led by the U.S., which withdrew from the World Health Organization, or WHO, officially in January 2026 . Other wealthy donor governments like Germany and the U.K. have also made cuts.
The WHO has warned that these cuts mean that in some places, the fight against polio will not be able to continue .
Only one human disease has ever been wiped off the planet for good: smallpox , in 1980. Polio could be the second . The world has never been this close.
Somewhere today, a healthcare worker is coloring another tiny pinkie purple. Each one breaks a link in the chain that polio needs to survive.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne’s notebooks reveal the strange workings of his imagination
articles.author:
<name>Robert S. Levine, Distinguished University Professor of English, University of Maryland</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-s-levine-2771509"/>
paras: After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 , 21-year-old Nathaniel Hawthorne returned to his family home in Salem, Massachusetts, to live with his mother and two sisters.

Over the next two decades, the aspiring author took on just two short-term jobs. Otherwise, he spent much of his time as a recluse: reading, taking long walks in Salem, socializing with a small group of friends, and writing stories and sketches from the third-story bedroom of the home he called “ Castle Dismal .” During that period and beyond, Hawthorne kept a series of notebooks, which scholars see as an important primary source for understanding the ideas and descriptions that informed his early writings and later novels.
Mainly, however, the notebooks served as a writer’s repository: Hawthorne could let his imagination wander freely without having to worry about being called unconventional, depressive or mad.

For over three decades as a Hawthorne scholar , I’ve used the notebooks – later titled “ The American Notebooks ” – to help me prepare editions and scholarly monographs. But I’ve long been intrigued by the notebooks’ shortest entries. Often no more than a single paragraph, they make up fewer than 10,000 of the 200,000 words found in “The American Notebooks.” They are weird and captivating, and in their own way seem like what we now call flash fiction or microfiction .

Hawthorne published collections of his tales and sketches in 1837 and 1846 , which included such macabre and bleak tales: “ Young Goodman Brown ,” “ The Minister’s Black Veil ” and “ The Birth-mark .” In 1850, at the age of 46, he published his first novel, “ The Scarlet Letter ,” which established him as one of the leading American writers of his day.

After Hawthorne’s death in 1864, his wife, Sophia , began transcribing “The American Notebooks” for The Atlantic Monthly. In the process, she grew fond of the fragments, likening them to sketches that bring us “so very near the creative soul of the artist.”
I have collected 200 of the most compelling of these fragments for an edition that was published by the Library of America in October 2026.
Consider the following fragment, which has no relation to anything that Hawthorne actually published:
“To have one event operate in several places – as, for example, if a man’s head were to be cut off in the town, men’s heads to drop off in several other towns.”

Phrased as if for a story that would never be written, this jotting, complete in itself, conjures an eerie world in which violence toward one person reverberates through other people in other places, leaving human bodies mysteriously linked.
In a fragment written in 1836, Hawthorne fantasizes about upending social conventions:

“Would it not be wiser for people to rejoice in all they now sorrow for? – and vice versa. To put on bridal garments at funerals, and mourning at weddings. For their friends to condole with them, when they attained riches or power, as only so much care added &c.”

Hawthorne never wrote a story about women wearing bridal garments at funerals. But the stand-alone fragment, in the seeming spirit of Franz Kafka’s surreal and unsettling fiction , links success to misery, and happiness to death.

That Hawthorne could be regarded as a precursor to Kafka, who wrote posthumously published fragments , was first articulated by the Argentinian modernist Jorge Luis Borges in his 1949 lecture “ Nathaniel Hawthorne .” For Borges, Hawthorne prefigured Kafka in his commitment to “pure fantasies that do not look for a justification or moral and that seem to have no other substance than an obscure terror.”
Borges’ assessment seems especially apt for the parables, fantasies and fragments that can be found in Hawthorne’s “American Notebooks,” many of which evoke a hidden menace or unsettling plot:
“Follow out the fantasy of a person’s taking his life by installments, instead of at one payment – say ten years of life alternately with ten years of suspended animation.”
“Little gnomes dwelling in hollow teeth; they find a tooth that has been plugged with gold, and it serves them as a gold mine.”
In a longer fragment, written in 1853, Hawthorne anticipates the many horror films featuring a demonic or possessed child:

“A family, consisting of a father, mother, and two children, are out for a walk, and sitting together in a wood. The little girl rambles away into the wood – they call for her – within a brief time, she comes back. At first, they notice no difference in her; but by degrees, they begin to see something odd – they notice more and more, till, in the course of years, they almost suspect that it was not their own child, but a strange child, who came back.”

Hawthorne, who had two daughters and a son, captures how children can seem to their parents like mysterious little people beyond their control. He would explore this dynamic in Pearl, the willful child in “The Scarlet Letter.” At one point, Pearl’s mother, Hester Prynne, wonders whether she’s a “demon offspring.”

Hawthorne’s notebook fragments are wide-ranging, but certain themes repeatedly crop up: the psychology of divided selves, tensions between men and women and even possibilities for a better world. As he hopefully imagines in a stand-alone fragment: “Cannon transformed to church-bells.”

Who was Hawthorne the writer? A neo-Puritan moralist? A social realist? A modernist? A romancer? The fragments complicate rather than answer such questions. In his preface to “ The Scarlet Letter ,” Hawthorne remarks on his desire to “keep the inmost Me behind its veil.”
But with the help of the fragments, we get behind the veil, at least a bit – and glimpse something like what Sophia believed was the spirit informing Hawthorne’s writing.

articles.title: I composed music about infertility and pregnancy loss, then performed it in a Pittsburgh hospital
articles.author:
<name>Katherine Pukinskis, Assistant Professor of Music, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katherine-pukinskis-2767318"/>
paras: It turns out you can rent a Steinway piano and have it delivered pretty much anywhere – including the lecture hall of a major working hospital.

In October 2025, I had one delivered to UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital in Pittsburgh for the premiere of “ One in Four, One in Eight ,” a 60-minute piece I composed about infertility and pregnancy loss, told through music, art, dance and narration.

Every October, families across the U.S. mark Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month , first proclaimed in 1988. This year, the observance arrives as federal funding cuts threaten reproductive health research , according to a report from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. That matters because so much about why pregnancies end, or never begin, is still unknown.

“One in Four, One in Eight” is built around a piano quartet – piano, violin, viola and cello – with artwork and choreography woven in. The music creates a space to explore something deeply personal and physical that is often invisible from the outside and stigmatized. The project brings together the human and emotional sides of infertility and pregnancy loss with the procedural and scientific ones.
The piece takes its title from two statistics : 1 in 4 known pregnancies ends in loss in the U.S. , and 1 in 8 women needs medical intervention to become and stay pregnant.

I am 1 in 4. I am 1 in 8. I’ve experienced the physical, emotional, social, financial, professional and psychological costs of infertility and pregnancy loss. As an assistant music professor and composer of contemporary classical music, I draw heavily on my own experiences as sources of inspiration; my creative practice is my research. But I also often consult external sources to inform aspects of my creative work.

The piece has four movements, each tied to a stage or experience common in infertility or pregnancy loss. Before each one, a narrator lays out the scientific context of these deeply personal experiences.

The narrations drew on interviews with Dr. Gabriela Gosman , Dr. Pamela Parker , Dr. Allison Serra and physician assistant Carrie Weaver , all reproductive care providers at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital. They also drew on research from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine , the National Institutes of Health , the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization . Gosman reviewed and approved every narration for medical accuracy.

The first movement, “Antecedent,” is about anticipation and potential energy. Its narration presents pregnancy as a societal ideal, while noting that a live birth depends on a monthslong chain of events going just right. The music is bright and open-ended, invoking the best-case scenario. Even when it stalls, nothing is fully lost – listeners can still find a beat and tap along.

The second movement, “Fissure to Flow,” explores the friction between the body’s natural cycles and assisted reproductive technologies , or ART, which suppress and override those cycles. Pregnancy usually runs on its own clock, taking about 40 weeks from conception to birth. With ART, simply reaching a confirmed pregnancy can take months. Each round of in vitro fertilization, or IVF, is timed to a menstrual cycle, and doctors sometimes stop a round partway through, such as when the ovaries don’t respond as expected to medication. Up to 20% of rounds are stopped before eggs are ever retrieved, which means more waiting and starting over. Some people succeed after one round of IVF; others after several. Some never do.
Musically, in this movement, the four instruments playing gradually line up until they suddenly lock in, revealing how unsettled everything sounded before.
The third movement, “Somatic Drift,” is about loss and being lost. The music feels both aimless and intensely focused.

Pregnancy loss can stem from chromosomal or structural abnormalities, such as a uterine septum , fibroids or scar tissue . It can also stem from hormone imbalances involving prolactin or progesterone .
Yet about half of all pregnancy losses are unexplained . That’s not because there is no cause, but limited research and funding leave doctors with few tools to find one.

The final movement, “Fortified,” is about the calm that comes with information, though this doesn’t make it a happy ending. Its grounded music acknowledges the financial, physical, emotional and professional costs of infertility and pregnancy loss . The narration highlights changes in care I hope to see, from better pain management for invasive procedures to in-office childcare for last-minute appointments, along with new research and legislation to support ART.

To be fortified is to be made stronger. Bodies hold on to pregnancy, too. Cells from a pregnancy can remain in a person’s body for years afterward, whether the pregnancy lasted four days or 40 weeks. This is a phenomenon called fetal microchimerism .

“One in Four, One in Eight” was designed to reach beyond a typical concert audience. Alongside the music and the narrated science, the performances featured the San Antonio-based chamber ensemble Agarita Chamber Players , who performed the piece, along with choreography by Pittsburgh-based Attack Theatre and new visual art works by Pittsburgh visual artist Morgan Overton . Both Attack Theatre and Overton created their work in response to the music, and it debuted live during the performances.

To make the concerts easier to attend, tickets and on-site childcare were free, and the project paid for parking. Before each concert, the project team hosted talks with me and the other artists to welcome people into the conversation. Afterward, receptions gave nonprofit community organizations space to share information and resources.

The science and music in “One in Four, One in Eight” depend on one another. Where a clinical setting is a crucial component of health and healing, public performances create spaces for learning, understanding and catharsis.
Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania .

articles.title: 50 years later, Amory Lovins’ soft energy path meets electrification
articles.author:
<name>Daniel Cohan, Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/daniel-cohan-201120"/>
paras: Hurricane Belle was barreling toward New England in August 1976 when an editor from Foreign Affairs called. Physicist Amory Lovins took the call on a payphone in a shack in the Maine woods, where he spent summers as a camp guide.

“If it happened to hit that area, the wires would be down with trees on them for weeks, so we’d miss the press date,” Lovins told me in a 2025 interview. The lines held up as he and the editor worked through final edits on a 14-hour phone call.
Published in October 1976 in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, “ Energy Strategy: The Road Not Taken? ” drew more reprint requests than any Foreign Affairs article in decades .

Two U.S. Senate committees called on the 29-year-old Lovins to testify about his ideas that December . The following year, Lovins met with President Jimmy Carter and his top energy advisers in the Oval Office and expanded his article into a book, “ Soft Energy Paths: Toward a Durable Peace .” The New York Times chronicled the “raging debate” sparked by Lovins, noting that “ even his critics concede that he is something of a genius .”

The article charted two paths for the future of energy. One, which Lovins called the “hard” path, required ever more energy supply to meet inexorably rising demand. With U.S. oil production in decline since 1970 , coal and uranium would supply most growth by generating electricity at large, remote facilities.

Lovins instead championed a “soft” path that put people’s wants ahead of supplies. “ People do not want electricity or oil … but rather comfortable rooms, light, vehicular motion … and other real things,” he wrote.

The soft path would meet those wants with a diverse array of renewable energy resources, sourced locally where possible. Heating would come from solar collectors and waste heat. Vehicles would be made more efficient and run on biofuels. Wind power would be used to compress air to drive machinery. Oil and gas would be reserved for making chemicals. Lovins hoped that matching form with function could enable U.S. energy use to plateau and then decline so that it could be supplied renewably by 2025.

When Lovins wrote his article, most electricity was generated inefficiently from fossil fuels or uranium, while wind and solar power remained prohibitively expensive. “Photovoltaics were out of bounds intellectually; that gets you laughed out of the room, and I didn’t actually think they would get cheap enough,” Lovins told me in 2025.

Burning or fissioning a fuel to generate electricity inefficiently, transmitting it far away, and turning it back into low-grade heat for homes was “ like cutting butter with a chainsaw ,” Lovins wrote. Thus, his soft path included only a narrowing lane for electricity, steering it toward essential purposes such as electronics, subways, lighting and smelting. Lovins posited that “ an affluent industrial economy could advantageously operate with no central power stations at all,” though he did not advocate going that far.

They were paths, not predictions, and neither path foretold the road actually taken in the 50 years since. Unlike most forecasts from the era, which projected ever-rising demand, the soft path foresaw that total U.S. energy use could plateau, and it almost exactly matched the actual level in 2000 . However, Lovins and his contemporaries failed to foresee the drilling advances that have kept oil and gas dominant.

As an environmental engineer completing a book about the visions that are shaping energy realities and opportunities around the world, I think Lovins got it half right about how to secure sustainable energy. Efficiency and renewable energy are indeed essential, but clean electricity and electrification are proving far more important than Lovins expected.

Critics argued that Lovins underestimated the costs of clean technologies and overstated what they could achieve. In fact, opportunities for clean energy have been transformed by unanticipated plunges in the costs of wind and solar electricity , battery storage and LED lighting .

For example, the price per watt of solar panels tumbled from around US$100 in current dollars in 1976 to around 10 cents in global markets today and a President Donald Trump-set minimum price of 38 cents for panels imported to the United States .

Modern technologies turn the chainsaw analogy on its head by making electrification the soft path to reducing energy use. Heat pumps supply several times as much heat as the electricity they consume. Induction stoves cook food far more efficiently than gas flames. And electric vehicles are a few times more efficient than gasoline ones.

Powered by renewable electricity, from local resources like the solar panels on Lovins’ roof and mine, or from larger solar, wind and geothermal facilities, these technologies can slash fossil fuel use. A diversity of resources blended with high-voltage transmission and storage can make clean electricity available around the clock .

When I visited Lovins’ ultra-efficient, solar-powered Colorado home in 2025, electrification took center stage. It was the induction stove that he showed off first, boiling water at lightning speed, then the batteries in the utility room. Two electric cars were charging outside. The wood stoves had been retired.

Former colleagues of Lovins now advocate an “ electrotech revolution ” centered on renewable electricity and increased electrification. Lovins told me he embraces their work but is pushing them to add integrative design — optimizing efficiency by redesigning whole systems — a subject he teaches at Stanford .
I believe Lovins was right to focus on matching resources with people’s actual needs. Renewable electrification and efficiency provide the softest path to doing so for the next 50 years.
Daniel Cohan interviewed Amory Lovins three times while writing two books.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: $137M spent on AI-generated midterm ads, and most voters can’t spot the fakes
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: The midterm elections are around the corner, and campaigns and PACs have already spent more than $137 million to air AI-made ads, including an 85-second video in which Texas Senate candidate James Talarico looks into the camera, reads his old tweets aloud, and voices spicy commentary he never actually made. The Senate Republicans’ campaign arm produced it. UC Berkeley deepfake expert Hany Farid said most people wouldn’t immediately know it was fake; the “AI GENERATED” tag sits small and faint in a corner.

Between now and Nov. 3, any clip of a candidate on your TV or in your feed may be fabricated, and most carry no AI label whatsoever. I’ve been predicting a deluge of deepfakes, and fear that it will get worse if we don’t act.

In 2024, I donated a year of my life to fighting political deepfakes by founding the nonprofit TrueMedia.org. A talented team at TrueMedia.org developed a state-of-the-art deepfake detector in record time and distributed it broadly, free of charge. It analyzed more than 60,000 images, videos and audio clips in elections worldwide, but it was early.

The Wesleyan Media Project, which reported the $137 million figure, found less than $50,000 in AI ad spending for the entire 2024 cycle. In January 2025, I said , “It did not materialize in 2024. That doesn’t mean that it’s not coming.” We open-sourced the technology and transferred it to Georgetown University, which resurrected TrueMedia.org in time for the peak of the current election cycle.
I was expecting foreign operatives to be the most prolific fakers. But in 2026, the deepfakes are coming from American campaigns and PACs, on television and in your feeds.

Many of the AI ads the Wesleyan Media Project has cataloged are harmless. Some are cosmetic: a still photo of Oklahoma candidate Chip Keating animated into a smile, or a synthetic family at a kitchen table where a campaign used to buy stock footage. Fred Davis, who has made campaign ads for 50 years, told The New York Times a scene that would have cost $2 million to shoot now costs about $200,000 to generate. Nobody is deceived.

Others are absurd on their face: New York’s governor and mayor gardening together while pitching a “political delusion pill” in a Bruce Blakeman campaign ad, or Spencer Pratt as Batman leading fed-up Angelenos armed with tomatoes. Pratt finished third in the Los Angeles mayoral primary. These are political cartoons with a pulse, and they’re protected satire. NYU’s Scott Babwah Brennen calls the genre “AI-generated slopaganda”: political slop made to stir feelings rather than make an argument.

The third kind is built to be believed, like the Talarico video. A Make Oklahoma Great Again PAC ad showed gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei cheek to cheek with Hillary Clinton under the words “Clinton Lover. Trump Hater,” with no AI label; the PAC spent more than $200,000 putting it on Oklahoma television. A PAC ad in Minnesota showed Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan with her hand out in front of a pile of cash. Talarico’s own ad now ends with the words “Made by humans, not A.I.”

A deceptive fake doesn’t need to be high quality. In a 2021 experiment with 5,750 people, a deepfake of Elizabeth Warren convinced 47% that a fabricated scandal was real; a plain fake headline convinced 43%.

A Utah Valley University study this June found voters identified deepfakes correctly about 16% of the time, and people who called themselves “extremely familiar” with deepfakes did no better than people who said they weren’t familiar at all. Media literacy doesn’t inoculate you against deepfakes.
The laws on the books fail to solve the problem. At least 31 states have deepfake election statutes. Wesleyan’s researchers found 29% of AI ads labeled in states with laws and 32% in states without.

Even when a label appears, voters often miss it. NYU’s Center on Technology Policy showed 1,051 people labeled and unlabeled ads. Thirty-seven percent didn’t remember seeing Michigan’s required disclaimer at all, and because it says “manipulated by technical means” rather than “AI,” only 21% identified AI as the technology involved. The one thing labels reliably did was make viewers trust the candidate who ran the ad less, which is why campaigns leave them off.

My proposed solution is simple: the litmus test should be the person shown, not the technology used. Did a real person agree to be shown this way? If not, the ad carries a plain-language label, on screen and in the audio, or it doesn’t air. A station manager can apply the test in a minute, which addresses the complaint that nobody can define “deceptive.” The rule should cover paid political ads, the one place a broadcaster already checks every spot before it airs; memes, satire accounts and your cousin’s group chat are a different problem.

Sejin Paik, the Georgetown researcher who now leads TrueMedia, puts the television problem plainly: “On TV, where AI ad spending is rising, a viewer watching a deceptive ad has little room for a crowd reaction or a provenance mark to change their view.”

H.R. 9922 would set a federal disclaimer rule, and the consultants’ own trade group is asking for a federal standard to replace the state patchwork. When the regulated party asks for the regulation, pass it.

Voters are ahead of Congress: in a Scripps News poll this month, 43% of registered voters said they had already been fooled by an AI-made ad this campaign, and 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want rules on AI in politics.

Looking to the future, the 2028 election is a presidential one — we don’t want to be flooded with even more deceptive AI ads. Two years is enough time to get the rules and processes in place, if we start now.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Stop MAGA from Taking Over Washington, Vote No on I-645, I-001, and I-638
articles.author: Suresh Chanmugam
paras: I was born and raised in Baton Rouge, Louisiana to immigrant parents. I moved to Seattle in 1999 to work as a software engineer in large part due to the progressive values cultivated by Washington State. My wife and I are grateful to the communities and culture here, where we’ve been able to raise three children who attend public schools in diverse communities. One of the reasons we are raising our kids here is Washington’s commitment to inclusion. Our state was one of the first to pass marriage equality, and we have strong laws against discrimination.

I deeply appreciate that the tech industry in Washington is considered a safe, welcoming place for LGBTQIA+ people, particularly our transgender friends and colleagues, who face escalating threats to their very right to existence. More parents, including many of our tech colleagues, say they are moving here to protect their children from draconian laws that are linked to increases in suicide rates.

But, near-trillionaire Elon Musk is fanning the flames against the transgender community by spending hundreds of millions of dollars through his “America PAC” (political action committee) running anti-trans political ads in elections around the country to try to drive swing voters to vote Republican. Most voters agree that this strategy is using hate to try to distract us from the high cost of groceries, gas, housing, and healthcare.

Now, right here in blue Washington State, multi-millionaire hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, through his PAC Let’s Go Washington, is using the same MAGA playbook. Heywood and his posse of right-wing uber rich supporters are bankrolling three harmful ballot measures before Washington voters this election, and two of them put a target on the backs of LGBTQIA+ children, a particularly malicious tactic.

Initiative 638 (IL26-638 on your ballot) is the most extreme policy of its kind in the country, and that’s saying a lot when red states like Idaho, Florida, Tennessee, Kansas, Utah, and Iowa have passed dozens of laws restricting civil rights, freedoms and access to care for transgender people. To exclude and humiliate trans girls from sports, I-638 would require all girls to undergo sex inspections to play elementary, middle, or high school sports.

Doctors say to be in compliance with this new rule, they will have to conduct invasive genital exams on young girls or expensive genetic and hormone testing that is unlikely to be covered by insurance because it is not medically-necessary. (And in blatant discrimination, only girls would be required to undergo potentially harmful sex inspections because the initiative exempts boys.)

Initiative 001 (IL26-001) is an anti-parents rights, anti-LGBTQIA+ measure. As a parent of three Seattle Public Schools teenagers, I know the facts: parents already have the right to information about their child, including the right to opt them out of certain curriculum or programs, and to talk to teachers, school counselors or nurses about their concerns.

While most kids have a safe loving home, sadly not all do. There were more than 115,000 reports of child abuse in Washington state in 2024 alone. As someone deeply involved with work to address our housing crisis, I have seen that the majority of homeless youth are LGBTQIA+ kids who have been kicked out or left their home because they didn’t feel safe there. I-001 will make this crisis worse, and is a direct threat to the safety of vulnerable young children who need confidential access to trusted, trained professionals like school counselors.

Initiative 645 (IP26-645) is an extension of Musk and the billionaire bros who successfully lobbied the Trump administration for policies that benefit themselves, Heywood is also trying to buy a tax cut for himself and other extremely wealthy individuals by repealing Washington’s new millionaires tax. The tax itself is very popular with the majority of voters in part because it pays for B&O tax cuts for small businesses (including small tech startups) and cuts the regressive sales taxes that impact working families. It raises billions for schools, childcare, free meals for K-12 students, and tax rebates for working families.

Having grown up in Louisiana, a state notorious for underfunded public schools, it’s appalling to me that Washington’s public school system isn’t much better. Our schools are chronically underfunded due to our state’s upside down tax code and I-645 will make it worse.

I’m tired of the false narrative that workers and businesses are leaving the state because of the millionaires tax. Skilled workers don’t want to leave Washington and move to Tennessee or Texas where they could face jail time and even death because they had a miscarriage. In fact, Starbucks, Oracle, and others have struggled to convince their employees to leave Washington. Over 100 Seattle Starbucks employees chose to have their job eliminated rather than move their family to a red state. Oracle moved its headquarters to Nashville and added only seven net new employees there last year. Austin is declining as a tech hub.

The Seattle metro region is the second largest tech hub in the country, but passing these initiatives would risk a tech talent flight to communities with stronger human rights protections like the Bay Area, New York City, Boston, and Northern Virginia. Political initiatives like I-645, I-001, and I-638 aren't just harmful to marginalized members of our community; they're also bad for business.

I urge my tech colleagues to say no to Brian Heywood and his attempt to distract us from the real problems caused by MAGA politicians, like exorbitant groceries, escalating rents, disappearing health care, and a reckless war that has killed innocent civilians and caused permanent destruction of business data that was supposed to have 99.999999999% (11 nines) of durability . Rejecting Heywood’s initiatives is one way we can protect all children’s rights, health, safety, educational, and economic opportunities.
Suresh Chanmugam has worked as a software engineer in Seattle since 1999 and is a steering committee member of Tech 4 Housing .
Editor's note: The Urbanist Elections Committee also endorsed a "no" vote on Initiatives 001, 638, and 645 .

articles.title: Op-Ed: Prop 1 Will Sustain Seattle's Transit Momentum
articles.author: Ashwin Bhumbla
paras: It cost me three dollars to get to City Hall the day I joined many others to fight for the future of Seattle transit. An Uber would have been a little faster but much more expensive at twenty dollars. I could've used a Lime bike, but it would've taken longer and, again, would have been more expensive at around fifteen dollars. Maybe I could've driven, but like 20% of households in Seattle , I don't own a car. I shudder to think how much purchasing one for that drive would've set me back.

So, I left the cafe I was working from and despite having recently missed a bus, I had to wait only seven minutes until the next one arrived. I hopped on the Route 7 and in about twenty minutes I was at City Hall along with dozens of others to advocate for a strong Seattle Transit Measure renewal in front of City Council . The trip was affordable, safe, fast, and easy.

After listening to over an hour of public testimony, it was clear that transit advocacy was only scratching the surface of reasons folks relied on the bus. I heard workers in tech, healthcare, service, public works, manufacturing, and trade describe the route they relied on to get to work. I heard seniors who could not afford to or who were unable to drive speak glowingly of the bus that took them to groceries, healthcare visits, and to resource centers. I heard union workers speak to what working for the transit system meant to them and their families. Speaker after speaker remarked on how they would not be able to afford to get to the places they needed to go without the bus. Finally, I heard a commenter describe how they relied on the bus for love, taking it to a first date – drawing the loudest cheer from the crowd of the day.

The advocacy that day succeeded. The measure we were fighting for survived being watered down and is now on your ballots. For a more affordable, sustainable, and accessible city, and for every person, I heard that day, and in the many days since, I’m voting yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and to expand and improve our incredible transit system.

Before asking you to do the same, perhaps some background context would be helpful. The Seattle Transit Measure (STM) renewal will authorize the city to collect a 0.3% sales tax for 10 years, collecting approximately $138 million annually. This is an increase from the current STM which is a six year sales tax (2020 to 2026) at a 0.15% sales tax rate, generating around $50 million annually. These funds will be spent on a variety of transit-related investments, but will be primarily used to bolster bus service in Seattle.

I believe passing this measure will improve the lives of every Seattleite. I have faith in this prediction as the best predictor of the future is the past, and by every metric, the current STM has been a massive success. It passed in 2020 with a staggering 80% of the vote! But its electoral success does not matter as much as what it actually did . The enormous faith voters placed in the measure has more than paid off, and renewing the measure will continue to build on that momentum. We can see this by breaking down what that money was spent on and what it achieved.

While bus service is provided by King County Metro and thus funded by a county-wide 0.9% sales tax, demand for transit service in Seattle has been higher than the baseline service Metro provides. This is the primary reason why the Seattle Transit Measure was first passed in 2014, passed again overwhelmingly in 2020, and why it should be approved again now.

One out of every 15 buses (approximately 180,000 annual trips) that run in Seattle are currently funded by the STM. That is a massive amount of trips that the STM has delivered every year of its existence.

More buses are better for everyone. For transit riders, increased frequency and reliability means more flexibility and less stress. Frequency is freedom and expanding when and how often a bus runs makes transit more viable as a primary mode of transportation. That makes things better even for drivers as the more people that take the bus– with fewer driving cars, the roads will be safer and less traffic-heavy.

Finally, more transit service is a necessity. From a sustainability standpoint, reducing the total number of vehicles on the road is the single most impactful thing our city can do to reduce its emissions. From a logistics standpoint, the city keeps growing, adding thousands to its population every year. However, we have limited street space. There simply is not room to add more cars to this city at the rate people currently drive. To continue Seattle's growth, we need to make transit a more viable mode of transportation. The current STM has made enormous strides in this regard. Unfortunately, it's still not enough.

Seattle wants more transit service because it needs more transit service. Due to funding issues caused by the Covid-19 pandemic as well as funding and operator availability issues from King County Metro, total bus service is actually at a lower level than it was pre-pandemic in 2019. We are down from 70% of the city having access to ten minute frequency service to approximately 53% . Transit demand has shifted, no longer only commute-based, but also with greater demand being seen for increased frequency on weekends, evenings, and nights. Late night service remains sparse. SDOT's Frequent Transit Network (FTN) , its aspirational goal in service of addressing these shortcomings, is still not fulfilled.

This is where the STM renewal comes into play. The renewal, with its increased funding, will almost double the amount of bus trips added by the current STM, going up to 275,000 trips added annually. It will focus on filling gaps in the FTN, adding additional trips on key routes on off-peak hours. Seattle is a city that does not only exist to go to work and this measure will help make transit a more viable option for every transportation need at all times of the day.

Seattle residents won’t have to wait years to see the benefits. If this measure passes, these additional trips will be phased in relatively quickly as part of Metro's twice-yearly service changes. Metro has confirmed that it is coming out of the operator shortage it has been facing the past few years and stands ready to not only increase its baseline level of service but also fulfill the additional trips that Seattle would be purchasing should STM be renewed. Every additional bus trip funded means that the most affordable transportation option becomes more viable for more people.

It's also important to note that King County Metro, as the operator of the buses, is most directly responsible for safety and security on those buses. By purchasing all this additional bus service, a portion of every transit service purchase goes directly to Metro's safety and security programming. In 2025, 6.3% of STM funds were spent on Metro's safety initiatives. The renewal, by increasing investment in bus service, will continue and expand this investment and continue to make the safest mode of transportation even safer.

On top of bus service, the STM has funding for capital projects to unlock more transit service and make it safer and more reliable. The current STM funded projects such as adding bus lanes on Rainier Ave (which increased performance for riders of the Routes 7, 48, and 106) or contributing funding to the RapidRide J line. While not directly funded by the STM, the recent Denny Way Bus Reliability Project , is another example of the immediate relief that targeted capital projects can provide, having quickly and effectively improved the reliability of both the Route 8 bus. The STM renewal will continue to have funding for capital projects such as these to ensure that buses can run faster, making every dollar invested in transit service go farther.

The current STM also expands access to transit by ensuring that those who need assistance the most can afford to use it. Through the Transportation Access Programs (TAP), STM currently provides around 10,000 free ORCA cards for residents of Seattle Housing Authority, Seattle Promise Scholars, and Seattle Preschool Program families who attend tuition free.

The STM renewal would more than double the amount of ORCA card recipients, going to 22,000 total. While transit is already vastly more affordable than owning and operating a personal car ( which now costs an average annual amount of over twelve thousand dollars nationwide and shows no sign of decreasing, as gas prices continue to climb), there are still many in this city to whom the cost is a barrier. STM and its renewal do not only expand transit, they expand access to transit, which is just as essential.

While buses consist of the majority of transit investments, the STM also funds essential transit services such as the First Hill and South Lake Union Streetcars, Trailhead Direct, and on-demand Metro Flex services.
The STM renewal will continue these investments to ensure that transit access is spread as far as possible.

The STM is a great piece of legislation. It has delivered immediate returns to the taxpayers that overwhelmingly voted it in and its renewal will make its investments even stronger. Investing in stronger, more accessible transit service pays dividends for affordability, safety, livability, and local economy. The more people can afford to safely get where they live and work and play, the better our city becomes.

The impact of an increase to an already high local sales tax cannot be ignored. Unfortunately, until state law changes, sales tax is the most viable method of funding transit service. The STM renewal and its increase of 0.15% to the sales tax rate would be estimated to cost the average Seattle median two-person household an additional $29 per year - even less for many single-person and lower-income households. In an earlier op-ed , the MASS coalition put this cost into context by comparing it to 4 hours of parking, one hour of riding a Lime, a 30 minute uber, a tank of gas, or one week of car ownership.

The purpose of such a comparison is not to make light of what a tax increase means to people at a time where every dollar needs to go the furthest it possibly can. On the contrary, the comparison shows what a good investment the STM renewal truly is and how affordable investment in transit is when compared to other transportation options. If we do not renew the STM, we will face drastic guaranteed transit service cuts. The hit to transit service and the increased cost of relying more on other modes of transportation will far outweigh the cost of the measure.

Seattle is a world-class city with world-class transit, but it can be even better. Good public transit is not free, but it does bring freedom. Freedom to work, to shop, to seek help, to play; freedom from traffic and from never-ending car payments. Transit connects our city and connects people to the places they need to access in order to live their lives.

Sometimes in this city there is a sense that the Seattle Process™ can overwhelm us, slow things down, make it seem like actually changing anything is impossible. That building things is no longer feasible.

We can build, and not only that, we can build quickly and efficiently. Should the STM be renewed, its benefits will not potentially be felt a decade from now. It will be felt within months. Whether you are an avid transit user, driver, both, neither, or anywhere in between, vote Yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and help build our transit network to make this city more affordable, safe, and easy to navigate.

articles.title: Tom Skerritt Has Left the Grand Illusion
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Tom Skerritt died on October 21 of natural causes. He was 93. I last saw him in 2022 during a dinner party thrown by Michael Hebb on Vashon Island. Low clouds covered that mid-September day, but no rain fell. And Skerritt, who arrived at dusk, sat at the head of a table we shared with the choreographer Donald Byrd. The subject of the night was Generations Over Dinner .

His thoughts were not with the gathering of 10 or so people but somewhere deep within his mind. We spoke a little about this and that. He asked what I was working on, and after I gave him a brief summary of my doings, he politely receded to his thoughts. As the island’s sea-soaked dusk around us grew, and the conversation of human generations (those about to go, those who are new) expanded, Skerritt became more and more pensive. This was not the Skerritt I was accustomed to; the Skerritt who, as an educator and activist for local film production (he moved to the Seattle area in the late ’80s), was committed to everything that had to do with the art of motion pictures, particularly storytelling. This was the substance and vastness of the conversation I had with him in 2018 in a Lower Queen Anne cafe. We talked for nearly two hours, and I left his company feeling a bit special.

Skerritt first came into my world when I was just 10. He had a leading role in a movie, Alien , that, at the time (1979), was reported to be so frightening it caused a person to faint during a screening. More amazing yet, this person had to be carried out of the theater on a stretcher. I had to see this flick, but was prevented from doing so at the box office of a cinema close to my school, Janney Elementary, in Washington, D.C. It was rated R. I wasn’t even close to 17. No can do for you, my guy, said the box office clerk.

I finally watched the movie four years later on a video cassette I rented from a Harare video store (my family returned to Zimbabwe in 1981). And I was drawn not so much by the horror of the alien, which occupied the second part of the film, but the labor disputes that Skerritt’s character, the space-weary Captain Arthur Dallas, had to deal with. My Marxism was born around this time.

A few years after that, I saw Skerritt in the movie Top Gun , which played at a Harare movie theater, Rainbow Cinema. And six years after that (now back in the States), I caught him again in Singles (he played the mayor of Seattle), and also in Contact (he played a government bureaucrat who wasn’t as keen about this alien business as Jodi Foster’s character, Dr. Eleanor Arroway). Of course, these are only a few films in a career that spanned seven decades, and included hits and classics like M*A*S*H , The Dead Zone , Steel Magnolias , and A River Runs Through It . He had a good number of TV shows under his belt, the most noted of which is Picket Fences .

The last movie I saw Skerritt in was East of the Mountains , which my cousin S.J. Chiro directed. Based on a novel of the same name by David Guterson, and released in 2021, the film wasn’t easy to watch because of the directness of its subject and subject matter: an old man, Ben Givens, dealing with death, with personal extinction. As a consequence, Mountain contains moments when the difference between Skerritt and his character seem indistinguishable. Always, the one thing our minds can’t get around, can’t solve, can’t come to terms with is death. How can you be totally something today, and totally nothing tomorrow?

The first time I met Skerritt in person was in 2005, after my film Police Beat screened at SIFF. He attended the movie’s post-show party at Barcça Lounge. He walked through the door, spotted me with a big smile on his face, strided to me, and gave me the biggest hug ever. And he didn’t let go. And all I could think was: I’m finally in Dallas’s arms. Maybe it’s my turn to faint. Goodnight, Skerritt.

articles.title: Downtown Highrise Project Still Under Fire as Design Gets Revised Taller
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The property owners behind a potential cross-laminated timber highrise project in Downtown Seattle aren't shirking away in response to considerable pushback against their project – they're going taller. Plans shown this week to the Seattle Landmarks Board would still add a residential tower above a retrofitted Doyle Building at 2nd Avenue and Pine Street, but include six more floors than a proposal initially floated last year .

That change is only likely to intensify opposition to the project, with preservation advocates wary of seeing significant changes to the landmarked 1920 structure joining forces with nearby condo owners not happy about seeing a new tower creep up next door. If built, the new structure would extend 23 stories up alongside its neighbor, the 39-story 1521 2nd Avenue building.

Fana Group, which owns the Doyle Building, has enlisted a team that calls itself Buildings Reimagined – made up of the design firm Clark/Barnes and general contractor BN Builders – to rethink the future of the four-story structure. The Doyle would be converted into a concrete structure capable of supporting a mass-timber tower above, retaining only the north and east facades. A one-story gasket level would accommodate the transition to 18 stories above.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law , Washington cities can no longer require facade modulation or upper level setbacks with mass-timber developments projects or redevelopments that convert commercial space into residential. That means Seattle's existing tower spacing rules do not apply here, with an average distance to the 1521 2nd Avenue building of just under 21 feet. It also means that there are no variances being proposed by Clark/Barnes that could add additional red tape, with the landmarks approval process one of the only remaining barriers standing in the way of potential approval.

"By combining the preservation, the sustainable materials, innovative design, and construction talent, we're going to be able to add more housing downtown," W. Scott Clark of Clark/Barnes told the landmarks board Wednesday. "This is why we created Buildings Reimagined, to help distressed properties that are really challenged and also difficult to entitle, to demonstrate that preservation and financially viable development are not mutually exclusive, and that that they can benefit one another."

Historic preservation advocates apparently disagree. A group called "Save the Historic Doyle Landmark" has already sprouted up to oppose the project as presented, and the advocacy non-profit Historic Seattle sent out an action alert in advance of this week's meeting.

"While not a large or tall structure, the Doyle building has stood out through the decades as downtown has evolved, bearing witness to and surviving the boom-and-bust nature of this city. This human-scale, right-size, mixed-use building stands today due to its original high quality of design, construction, materials, condition, and integrity," Historic Seattle's email stated. "The proposal is to demolish most of the building, leaving only two facades standing, and erecting 23-stories of new residential construction behind the two facades. Let’s be clear. This is NOT an addition to a landmark. This is NOT adaptive reuse. This is NOT historic preservation. This IS facadism. If approved, this would be a demolition of most of the landmark."
But Clark pushed back on claims that they would be demolishing the Doyle this week, framing that as misinformation.

"We are not demolishing the building. We are keeping the two historic featured elevations on the two streets. [...] We are demolishing the alley facade and the roof, and we are going in and we're completely restructuring the interior of this building," Clark said. "Whether you're doing a one-story addition or a taller addition, you would need to reinforce the building to meet seismic. But given the loads that we're going to be subject to, we are going in and we're completely restructuring the internal of the building with a concrete structure."

One point of contention at the Landmarks Board is likely to be the massing of the upper story additions, which are only set back from the Doyle Building's cornices by about three-and-a-half feet. Multiple board members expressed concerns about this, especially as it relates to criteria set by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior on rehabilitation of historic structures. Criteria #9 states that new additions "will be differentiated from the old and will be compatible with the historic materials, features, size, scale and proportion, and massing" compared to the existing structure."

"What I've heard is that this has been scaled and designed to work with economics and making finances work. So as it stands, I have a lot of trouble supporting the project moving forward based on criteria number nine, and seeing that none of that has been applied to this project," board member Matthew Zinski said, referencing the gasket floor intended to be a break between the two segments of building. "Landmarks Board member Matthew Zinski said. "I struggle to see the design logic or what's being used there to help differentiate what's going on between the new addition and the existing building."
Clark defended the choice to extend the addition as far out as it's proposed, noting the limitations that are inherent on the site.

"I do have to say that we were dealing with the reality of a small [floor]plate. It's 8,900 square feet, and secondly, we had to deal with the condition of an eccentric core location, just given the overall dimensions and depths of the plate," Clark said. "We wanted to ensure that our unit layouts had the depth necessary to make comfortable living units, and so all of those things, all those very practical things, in conjunction with the vertical load path that we're trying to run through the building, in coordination with the structure, the existing structure of the landmark building really started to describe the overall mass and form of the building."
Board member Dan Sloat echoed concerns around the addition being too bulky.

"I really appreciate your discussion about the attempt to keep the the new tower structure visually quiet to create that contrast, and I think for me, the kind of equal proportioning of two parts fights against that a little bit," Sloat told Clark. "I'm having a hard time reading the visual quietness of the superstructure because it is so dimensionally similar to the structure below."

Wednesday's briefing, coming more than a year after the firm's first discussion with the Landmarks Board, still represents the early stages of the project. But the design team is heading toward applying for a Master Use Permit with the city, and is advancing forward. In the months ahead it will become clear just how much of an uphill battle getting final approval of the Landmarks Board will be.
But Clark clearly sees the project as a major benefit to downtown Seattle as a whole.

"[The Doyle building] really is at a crossroads, and we think what we're proposing is a very strong, responsible, and reasonable approach to revitalize the building and provide the needed housing downtown," Clark said.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Vote Yes on Prop 1 for More Buses!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Ballots for the November election have been sent to voters in King County. One item on the ballot for voters in Seattle is Proposition 1: Seattle Transit Measure. This renews and expands the Seattle Transit Measure that is set to expire in early 2027. The 0.3% sales tax is expected to generate $138 million per year that will fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years, 100,000 more bus trips than currently funded. It would also fund 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. Vote Yes to help fund transit in Seattle.

Since 2014, the Seattle Transit Measure has funded millions of bus trips in Seattle. Many of these trips are on weekends when most routes have less frequent service compared to weekdays. Route 36 is one such route that has received additional weekend trips. Between 2022 and 2026, the STM funded 22 additional trips on Saturdays and 42 additional trips on Sunday. In response, more people use Route 36 every weekend. Compared to 2022, Route 36 ridership on Saturday and Sunday has increased by 41% and 58%, respectively. Weekday ridership has increased 32%. This increased ridership represents more car-free trips and improved access to get to work, shops, and fun for people in Beacon Hill, Othello, and the International District.

The Route 36 success story is not an isolated one. Passengers on routes around Seatttle have benefited from additional service funded by the Seattle Transit Measure. Vote Yes to continue and expand the additional bus trips. Fill out your ballot soon and drop it off at one of the many ballot drop boxes in King County.

articles.title: New murals bring street art veterans and local roots to five Pike/Pine walls
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Five new murals are now looking out over Pike/Pine, painted by a crew of street art veterans and underground culture builders putting their imprint directly onto Capitol Hill’s everyday walls.

Led by On the Block and the Seattle Artist Coalition for Equitable Development , the “Paint the Block” initiative pulls from “renowned street legends with local longevity and deep neighborhood roots” to turn neighborhood walls into community infrastructure.

The five works span high-traffic corners and quieter stretches. Along the wooden exterior of the Wildrose at 1021 E Pike, Takiyah “TDUB” Ward painted For Shelley, The Wildest Rose honoring the late co-owner of the ‘Rose and urging the neighborhood to “Stay Creative.”
At 1200 E Pine, Myron Curry wrapped the parking bay of NW Liquor in bold scenes of drinks and street life, aiming to “inspire and empower communities through impactful cultural art.”

On a brick wall at 1016 E Pike, project curator Carolyn Hitt joined Maurice “REESBO” Kennedy on Time Traveling , which Kennedy celebrated as a chance to tell their stories in their “own stomping grounds — Capitol Hill.”
A few blocks west at 1426 Boylston Ave, Gerardo “Periko” Peña added a mural of an oversized blue cat Mina lounging among bright red blossoms.

Across from Cal Anderson behind 1535 11th Ave, a massive double piece brings Sam Sneke back to where he says he first “cut my teeth doing graffiti on Capitol Hill” three decades ago, pairing his Welcome to Capitol Hill with Pine Legacy B by SPECSWIZARD , BeSo 206 , and Brandon “ArtbreakerBT” Thomas , all sealed under clear coats brushed on by hip-hop veteran Silas Blak .
Organizers say placing this work front and center sparks foot traffic and safety from the ground up.

“The Seattle underground and behind the scenes is vibrant,” Hitt said. “More resources to these vital culture pockets would go a long way to nurture extraordinary talents that are currently struggling to create under the crushing weight of our economic times.”
Funded by the Seattle Office of Arts and Culture’s HopeCorps under District 3 Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth , the effort is fiscally sponsored by Northwest Film Forum .

Hollingsworth secured $250,000 in JumpStart funds last fall to “support murals in and around Cal Anderson Park” through the HopeCorps program and another $25,000 to fund the painting of the park’s bathroom.
In this year’s budget debate, 19 Capitol Hill and Central District organizations and businesses have joined a call to move $8 million in budget from hiring more cops to spending more on artists.

The mural project also expands on years of DIY work on 11th Ave, growing out of monthly street markets and Eleven:Eleven , the all-ages “little campus of autonomous art studios” opened by On the Block founder Hitt.

Up next, Phase Two of the project will roll out an interactive mobile heritage map on the Capitol Hill Arts District site, followed by artist-led walking tours woven into regular Second Thursday Capitol Hill Art Walks and Second Saturday On the Block markets.
