articles.title: Idaho Lawmakers Tried to Conflate Abortion with Human Trafficking and Seattle Attorneys Are Fighting Back
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: Three years ago, the Idaho state legislature passed a law making it illegal to assist minors in crossing state lines to access abortion care. In the paranoiac tradition of American anti-abortion policy, the law was rooted in a poorly disguised moral panic : It specifically banned “abortion trafficking”—the fictional concept of shadowy adults coercing minors into having abortions and abducting them to make it happen. This, obviously, is a problem that doesn’t exist, and would curtail the very real rights of minors and their allies, all while claiming to have children’s best interests at heart.

Now, a lawsuit spearheaded by the Seattle-based gender equality legal advocacy group Legal Voice is challenging Idaho’s law, and what comes next could impact access to abortion everywhere, for better or for worse. “Everyone wants young people to be healthy and safe, but this law, if it stands, will put them in danger and isolate them from trusted adults, which is what nobody wants,” says Wendy Heipt, senior litigation counsel at Legal Voice.

Idaho has a trigger law that immediately criminalized abortion when Roe v. Wade was overturned, but Idahoans seeking abortions commonly travel to states like Washington and Oregon for care, a dynamic that predates Roe ’s reversal and has stymied the efforts of anti-abortion activists, since freedom of movement is a constitutionally protected right. But by targeting young people’s access to abortion, Idaho lawmakers may have identified a loophole in their efforts to curtail abortion-related travel, one likely to be replicated elsewhere if it’s allowed to continue.

Legal Voice is arguing that Idaho’s travel ban blocks the First Amendment by preventing Idahoans from even discussing abortions across state lines. The law is also poorly written: it states that it’s illegal for an adult to “harbor” or “recruit” minors, but doesn’t give clear definitions for either term, which creates confusion both about following and enforcing the law. And then there’s that one pesky detail in the Constitution: the right to travel between states is a fundamental personal freedom, one that states with anti-abortion policies have struggled to successfully undermine, even as restrictive abortion bans have gone into effect since Roe v. Wade was overturned.

In an April memorandum requesting a summary judgment in the case, attorneys from Legal Voice, the Lawyering Project, and Stoel Rives LLP mapped out concerns the law raises about barring travel tied to health care when that treatment is legal in the destination state. “If states could prohibit such assistance, the right to travel would become meaningless in practice,” they wrote.
But if Legal Voice’s case prevails, it could set a useful precedent by affirming that an anti-abortion policy in one state can’t necessarily be enforced in another.

So far, Legal Voice and the case plaintiffs have secured an injunction to keep the law from going into effect. It was modified following an appeal to the Ninth Circuit and remains partially in place. Still, according to Legal Voice, “Under the current order, our clients can still provide information, encouragement, and financial resources to youth seeking abortion care.” Now back at the district court level, both sides have issued motions for a summary judgment, meaning a ruling could soon be issued, without the need for a trial.

Legal Voice’s plaintiffs in the case are Lourdes Matsumoto, a lawyer who needs to freely share abortion information in her work with young survivors of sexual assault and domestic violence; the Northwest Abortion Access Fund; and the Indigenous Idaho Alliance, which works with five Northwest tribes and connects pregnant people with abortion resources. “They serve indigenous communities throughout Idaho, including for health care autonomy, and they want to support people making their own decisions, including minors,” says Heipt. “And their family structure doesn’t always fit the way the laws are written.”

In choosing to target young people and the adults who support them, Idaho’s law isn’t unusual. It’s a common tactic in anti-abortion legislation (and anti-trans legislation, for that matter; the two are irrevocably intertwined ): Work your way up to targeting access to health care for everyone, but begin by eroding minors’ access. “That’s typically where it starts,” says Heipt. “If they are successful with minors, I can assure you that it will not stop with minors.”

Historically, anti-abortion activists have accomplished this through policies like parental notification laws, popularized even before the US Supreme Court overturned Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization . These laws required minors to involve their parents in decisions about abortion, or to make their case before a judge to get permission if involving a parent wasn’t possible.
Though it contains no real requirements for involvement from a caregiver, Idaho’s abortion travel ban has been justified, like parental notification laws, as a policy promoting parental rights.

But just as “abortion trafficking” isn’t a real problem, a parental rights framing around abortion doesn’t make much sense, either, since data shows most young people who seek abortion care voluntarily choose to involve trusted family members.

A study on parental involvement in minors’ abortion decisions, published in the Journal of Adolescent Health , found that most minors—64 percent—specifically shared their plans to seek abortion care with their mothers, and, intriguingly, that parental involvement did not automatically equate to greater confidence in pregnancy decisions. Even without parental support, 81 percent of young people had “high confidence” in their own decision-making around abortion; maternal involvement was “not significantly associated with having high confidence in the decision,” the researchers found.

This is a very different reality than the “abortion trafficking” Idaho’s travel ban has purported to solve. In fact, when the law was first introduced in the Idaho legislature, Idaho Anti-Trafficking Coalition executive director Jennifer Zielinski told the Idaho Statesman that conflating human trafficking with helping someone voluntarily seeking abortion disrupted actual efforts to stop trafficking and risked retraumatizing victims. While human trafficking does sometimes involve forced abortion or pregnancy as a tool of control, the Idaho law would do nothing to help. “It takes the true effort off course,” Zielinski told the paper.

Heipt agrees. “It really does a disservice to actual survivors of trafficking to call something ‘trafficking’ because you don’t like it,” she says. And even the bill’s proponents seemed to understand this: The law is no longer listed in Idaho state code under “trafficking.”
Whether a judge will view it that way remains to be seen. A decision in the case is expected early next year.

articles.title: Wilson Pledges 'Striking Progress' With Homelessness Shift
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: This week, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson announced a shift in the City’s strategy for addressing homelessness by executing a “neighborhood-centered, by-name” framework to help most effectively use the new shelter spaces that will continue to open next year.
By the end of this year, Wilson’s administration is on track to open over 400 new shelter units, with the promise of reaching almost 1,000 by the end of 2027.

“For years, mayors and their teams have come and gone, but the moral outrage of homelessness in one of the wealthiest cities in the richest country in the world has only worsened,” Wilson said at a press conference. “In the four years before I took office, unsheltered homelessness increased by over 50 percent. This is unacceptable”.
Wilson’s predecessor, Bruce Harrell, only added a net 13 units of shelter during his entire four-year tenure.

Similar outreach practices, based on the framework developed by non-profit Community Solutions , were used in the City’s JustCARE program developed during the Covid-19 pandemic to some success and the Washington Transportation Right of Way Encampment Resolution Program, which was also considered to be successful but took significant cuts from Washington state in its 2025-2027 budget.

Wilson plans to emulate the recent success of a small pilot implemented to get unhoused people living in Pioneer Square into shelter before this summer’s World Cup games. Of the 80 people identified by outreach workers, 47% had been homeless for more than three years and 77% suffered from addiction or mental illness. Even so, 70 of those 80 people were placed into shelter.

“The partners used a by-name list, identifying every individual living unsheltered in that area and offering wraparound support instead of repeatedly referring people between disconnected parts of the homelessness response system,” Wilson said. “This program was highly centralized, zeroing in on specific barriers that specific people faced and connecting them to the appropriate resource. And it was also successful because of space available at Bayside, the first major new site in my shelter acceleration initiative, which opened up in June.”

Lisa Daugaard, the co-executive director of Purpose Action Dignity (PDA), shared with The Urbanist that 78.3% of participants in the Pioneer Square pilot remained in shelter and off the streets four months later, with over 20% able to move on to permanent housing, showing a notable level of sustainment achieved by the approach.

The relative success of this pilot, a partnership between the Downtown Seattle Association and service providers such as PDA and REACH, showed that when a more focused effort was brought to bear to make appropriate offers of assistance, unhoused people in Seattle were willing to accept shelter and services.

“This idea that we have a lot of service-resistant people in our city I think is a myth, and it's not a thing,” said Jon Scholes, president and CEO of the Downtown Seattle Association. “If we offer the right thing, we offer the right service, if we understand who's out there, if we don't offer a one-size-fits-all, we can bring people inside instead of chasing them around the corner, down the block, or to the next park. So we know what works, and the big shift here is building on that, not making it the exception for how we address homelessness in this city, but making it the rule.”

Instead of doing another targeted pilot, Wilson is taking a bigger swing with her attempt to utilize this framework city-wide, with a neighborhood allocation of high support shelter spots. Neighborhood leaders and service providers will prioritize individuals with the greatest challenges who come to their attention for the new spots. This approach is only possible because of the high number of new shelter spaces expected to open within the next year.

Both Wilson and Scholes pointed out that the status quo of homeless sweeps, emergency room visits, and jail stays is very expensive, and providing the right kind of shelter and services, while also pricey, will ultimately save the City money.

Wilson referenced the success of Denver in using the Community Solutions framework to reduce their homelessness population by 64% in three years, which The New York Times recently touted as the right way to fix homelessness . But Denver paired the framework discussed above with greatly increased police enforcement , with some homelessness advocates going as far as to warn other cities away from using Denver’s approach.
Advocates in Seattle have mixed feelings about Wilson’s plan.

“Obviously, this is better than our current approach,” Jay, a regular volunteer with Stop the Sweeps, told The Urbanist . “It sounds like moving in the right direction. It's by no means stopping the sweeps.”

Jay said that Stop the Sweeps has always made the argument that while sweeps are cruel, inhumane, and possibly unconstitutional, they are also ineffective as an outreach method and a real waste of money. “I do think more and more people are starting to realize this,” Jay said.

But while Jay thinks that more coordination between outreach services, local businesses, and neighbors could lead to better service matching, they emphasized that the City continues to spend a large amount of money on simply sweeping unhoused people from place to place.
Wilson has committed to continuing the City’s sweeps.

“Our Unified Care Team has continued doing encampment removals at basically the same rate that they were doing removals before I entered office. We anticipate that the Unified Care Team will continue that work,” Wilson said. “As we're opening up new sites, the Unified Care Team is going to be able to make more meaningful offers of shelter and services to people in encampments all across the city. So I would expect and hope that means that we will have higher rates of navigating people into that shelter as opposed to them moving to the next block.”
But as Josh Feit in PubliCola reported , the Unified Care Team has actually done more than 150 full encampment removals so far this year, compared with 112 at this point in Harrell’s first year.

Councilmembers Dionne Foster, Bob Kettle, and Eddie Lin all attended Wilson’s press conference and expressed support for her plan – and the $37 million allocated in next year’s budget to pay for the new shelter the plan requires.

But just the night before, the Seattle City Council passed a suite of bills with the ultimate goal of making it nearly impossible for people to live in their RVs in Seattle. Sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss, this new legislation would initiate a new RV permitting program with many requirements and a one-time census to allow people to apply. As passed, people who miss the census will have no future opportunity to apply for an RV permit.
The legislation would also provide RV storage and open a second safe lot. Glassyards Commons , a site offering a combination of a safe lot and tiny homes, is planned to open next month.

Wilson did not provide all the funding for Strauss’s proposal in her proposed 2027-2028 budget, a decision about which Strauss said he is “highly disappointed”, even as he has indicated his intent to introduce a budget amendment to allow his legislation to be implemented as planned. He also claimed Wilson is “uncomfortable” addressing homelessness, in spite of the issue being central to her mayoral campaign last year.
At the city council meeting on Tuesday afternoon, Strauss touted his RV proposal as centering humans.

“The resulting package strikes an important balance between creating new resources to help people build pathways to housing, cutting red tape that often leaves us waiting for years for services to come online, and updating our regulations to better meet the moment our city is in,” Strauss said.

But advocates have said the permitting program is likely to increase the number of people unhoused and on the streets, which would directly work against Wilson’s efforts to reduce the number of people in Seattle without access to any shelter.

In response to the legislation’s likely passage, King County Councilmember Reagan Dunn expressed his intent to propose new legislation at the county level to “prevent Seattle’s homelessness crisis from spilling into neighboring communities.”
“The rest of King County is getting a signal from Seattle,” Jay told The Urbanist . ”If Seattle can pass this, everyone else is going to pass it.”
Indeed, at the beginning of September, after the Seattle city council had already begun discussions of Strauss’ proposal, the City of Kirkland passed a city-wide ban of RVs on public streets.
The bills related to Seattle’s RV permitting program passed 6-3, with the council’s three progressives – Councilmembers Foster, Lin, and Alexis Mercedes Rinck – voting against it.
When asked about the RV bills during the press conference, Wilson expressed several concerns, including legal risk, cost, and the challenges of implementing a complicated new program.

“I also have concerns about the human impacts,” Wilson said. “If this solution is something that basically is going to result in more people getting into unsheltered homelessness or simply being pushed out of the city, then that is not a success. So I'm committed to working with Councilmember Strauss and my other colleagues on the City Council to get to a workable solution.”
The RV permitting program is not planned to go into immediate effect, and Wilson expressed a desire to engage in a process to make some changes to the program.

Another possibility would be for Wilson to veto the legislation. While the relevant bills passed with a veto-proof majority, the council will be welcoming a new District 5 colleague onboard at the end of November once election results are certified. If Nilu Jenks , who is running in the progressive lane, assumes the seat, it’s possible the veto-proof majority will no longer exist.

However, the timeline might be too tight for this strategy to bear fruit, with Wilson having 10 days to act on the legislation once she receives it. Were Wilson to veto, the council would then have 30 days for a vote to reconsider the matter.
Regardless, Wilson is banking her future in politics on her success in grappling with a homelessness crisis that has stymied several of her predecessors.
“This is the kind of striking progress that we're going to make here in the Emerald City,” Wilson said. “Change is in the air.”

articles.title: Daylight Shines Between Scully and Noble in the 32nd District
articles.author: Oliver J. Moffat
paras: Some voters in the 32nd district might be stumped filling out their ballots. Long time Shoreline city council member, Keith Scully, is running against Danica Noble, an anti-trust attorney and PTA advocate for State Representative position 1 in the 32nd. Both candidates are Democrats, and on most issues, Noble and Scully are more likely to agree than disagree. But in closing arguments to voters at a recent candidate forum, some differences between the candidates emerged.

The two candidates faced off in a forum hosted by the local democrats at the Edmonds Library on Saturday . Washington’s 32nd legislative district spans from Northwest Seattle, through Shoreline, Mountlake Terrace, and into Edmonds and Lynnwood. Noble and Scully are running for a legislative position previously held by longtime state Rep. Cindy Ryu who is running to unseat Senator Jesse Salomon, a race that has gotten much more media attention.

At the Edmonds forum, when asked about the most important issues local voters are facing, both Noble and Scully named education funding at the top of the list. And both candidates support the Millionaires' Tax and say the state must do more to fix Washington’s regressive tax system. Both candidates have left-aligned positions on how to address the homelessness crisis.

Their overlapping positions have left some voters in the 32nd district undecided. But at the Saturday forum, some daylight –but not much– was visible between Scully and Noble. Noble repeatedly called for urgent action to regulate AI and hold Big Tech accountable. Scully, on the other hand, appeared to position himself as the more centrist of the two candidates.
If voters send him to Olympia, Scully promised ten years of consensus building to “finally” get progressive tax reform done.

In the closing weeks of the campaign, Scully said he’s been out doorbelling a lot, talking to voters — even Republicans. Although many Republicans refuse to talk to him, he has had conversations with MAGA voters. “I talked to extremists on the left and extremists on the right… They're willing to pay taxes, as long as they feel like the money's going to be spent wisely,” he said.

Scully believes progressive taxation could be a bi-partisan issue. “Taxes come up at doors all the time. Most people, even Republicans, believe it or not, want progressive taxation. They just don't trust that Olympia isn't simply going to layer progressive taxes on top of regressive taxes,” he said.
Scully wants to lower taxes on small businesses with high operating costs (like restaurants) by charging B&O taxes on profits instead of revenues; another tax reform policy that could win consensus.

Lowering property taxes is also politically popular. “Senior citizens, or anybody on a fixed income, are very concerned about property taxes continuing to go up, because when you're on social security… that doesn't go up commensurate with the increase in property taxes… it's the difference between living comfortably and barely getting by,” he said.

At earlier candidate forums, Scully has promised broad budget cuts. “So my top funding priority is balancing the state budget. And I propose doing that with a 3% across the board cut for all state departments, with 2 exceptions. And that's education funding and behavioral health funding,” Scully said at a candidate forum last summer .

At Saturday’s forum, he did not repeat that promise for across-the-board cuts. But he was asked to respond to critics on the left who worry about his consensus-driven approach and want a legislator who will deliver more than just incremental changes.

“We need advocates to be disruptive. And the electeds need to listen and decide where a disruptive measure is appropriate. I'm certainly not afraid to go against the trend. I've been the dissenting vote on numerous things, but I don't start from a place of destruction, because the job of an elected is to put the pieces back together. The job of advocates is to say, this is broken, and for us to listen and say, is that true? Is that true?,” Scully said.
Noble, on the other hand, is calling for urgent action, and took a more forceful tone.

Like Scully, Noble named education funding as a top priority. As a member of the Washington State PTA Advocacy Committee, Noble has long lobbied for improved school funding in Olympia. But Noble has made fighting big technology corporations the centerpiece of her campaign. She spent two decades as an attorney at the FTC doing consumer protection and anti monopoly work, most recently suing Facebook’s parent company Meta for using algorithms to harm children online.

Noble repeatedly circled back to the fight against big tech in her comments at the forum. When asked how she would balance the state budget while fixing Washington’s regressive tax system, Noble proposed bringing in new revenue by taxing social media companies that use addictive algorithms to harm children.

“That's something I talk about at the doors all the time. And this is one of the few places you might see a difference between Keith and I… Some of the wealthiest companies in the world have products here that they offer. They're not gonna pull Facebook out of this state if we tax them. We need an addictive algorithm tax to incentivize those companies not to keep our kids on for one more hour… Those companies can pay their fair share of taxes. They have a zero price product, but it's not free. Anybody who has a phone or a kid knows we've been paying with our attention, let's tax them on that,” she said.

Voters are concerned about affordability and Noble says powerful corporations are driving the crisis. “Employers… collect your data and use it to suppress your wages… Companies without your permission… buy your data… and use it to raise the prices that you pay… An airline will charge you more if they already know you're going to a funeral. That is an extractive and exploitive business model,” she said.

“Uber buys the credit reports of its drivers, and if you have a really high credit card debt, they give you a lower percentage of your wage. They give you a shorter route. They give you people who are less likely to be tippers,” she said.

“That's just one example”, she continued, “they will offer the nurses in the worst financial situations 50% of the wages of other nurses. These are extractive and exploitative business models that stem from us not having a right to our own data.”

Speaking about the academic and mental health crises facing students, Noble said, “a lot of that has to do with what they are experiencing online. And so last year I wrote a bill to get cell phones out of schools. Olympia turned that into a study! I'm running in part to help Olympia get over its study problem and start solving some of these technological problems.”

When asked why she believes the state legislature is the right venue to regulate borderless technology like AI, rather than leaving interstate commerce rules to the federal government, Noble said, “at the federal level, our leader has said, ‘it's a hoax. All we need to do is let these guys, you know, protect themselves.’ And he tried to prevent states from even having any chance to regulate AI.”

“The only meaningful place where regulation is happening for tech is at the state level. And of the 84 AI bills that were passed last year in the United States, almost all of them were passed by the freshman legislators, people who had not served before. People who came with ideas that had not yet been crushed… We need that work so urgently,” she said.

When she gets to Olympia, Nobel said one of the first things she wants to do, “is following something Oregon did: get private equity out of healthcare. It's not good for the patient, it's not good for the providers. It only makes Wall Street investors wealthy. And Oregon did that and their state is already saving money.”

Citing her tough-on-big-tech priorities, The Urbanist endorsed Noble in this race while criticizing Scully for using tree removal fees and hard-scape maximums to keep new, denser housing out of Shoreline’s low-density single-family neighborhoods. (I serve on the endorsement committee, one of 14 members who helped to make that pick.)
When asked to respond to The Urbanist’s endorsement of his opponent, Scully doubled down.

“I love that article… Because what you've got to do when you're in a governing body is to make compromises. and try to, you know, get all needs somewhere in the middle. And that means if everybody leaves a room irritated, it's probably been a good city council session. I don't think it's an either/or I think we can have both urban density and urban trees," Scully said. "And for me, I evolved a bit, and I came around to supporting density around the light rail stations as a prime value. But not exclusively in the single family neighborhoods, because building an asphalt-covered hellscape is not the goal. The goal is getting a livable urban city near light rail. And that does occasionally include sacrificing some density for tree protection, or for impervious surface, or for parks, or for any other things that aren't strictly housing, but nonetheless, make a city someplace you want to be.”

Scully was not the only candidate asked about the Urbanist’s endorsement. In her questionnaire to The Urbanist , Noble said she supports increased funding to expand transit options and safe sidewalks. She was asked how she planned to fund transit and pedestrian infrastructure when (according to the opinion of the questioner) “crumbling roads” in the 32nd district “desperately need basic maintenance.”

“I think my view for the community is to have one that is not built for cars and based on people who always have cars. One of the coolest things I learned while campaigning is how many houses are car-free in Mountlake Terrace,” she said.
By now, voters have their ballots and Saturday’s forum will serve as the candidates' closing arguments to voters: a video recording of the forum has been posted online .

articles.title: Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: Much like route 550 was to Bellevue, route 545 has been Redmond’s workhorse route. Redmond has a diverse set of transit options fanning out in every direction, even before it had the distinction of being a Link terminus. But the main regional service has always been route 545, which connects downtown Redmond to downtown Seattle. However, as with many ST express corridors, route 545 was intended to be an interim service until rail reaches Redmond. Route 545 was always planned on being discontinued with the start of East Link service to Seattle, with the 2 Line taking over the entirety of both routes 545 and 550. The original plan (developed as part of the first iteration of King County Metro’s East Link Connections plan) deleted the 545 and 550, with some of the freed up service hours being used to make the 542 frequent and replace 545 service to Bear Creek P&R. Route 554 (later renumbered 556) was also planned to be moved to Bellevue to fill a gap in service on Bellevue Way left by the removal of route 550. Former riders of these routes either take a more frequent bus to connect the 2 Line, or can just take the 2 Line on its own.

Sound transit first let riders formally have a say on the potential changes in early 2025 as part of their 2026 service plan, and have a say they did! They received more feedback on route 545 than any other route by far, with its feedback results showing about 14% of respondents providing feedback on route 545, the runner-up being route 550 with about 9%. The broad consensus of the feedback was clear: don’t delete route 545. Sound Transit was so moved by these results that they did not even propose any changes to route 545 at all in any of their own ST Express proposals, even while moving forward with major changes nearby such as deleting route 550 and combining route 554 with route 556, relying entirely on Link to get I-90 riders to Seattle.

The reasoning is sensible. The 2 Line crosses the lake along I-90, so buses heading to Seattle via I-90 are the most duplicative of rail, and forcing a transfer would add little travel time (or even save time in some cases). Route 545, on the other hand, has a straight shot to downtown Seattle via the 520 bridge. Trading that for a detour to I-90 through Bellevue would add travel time, and riders told Sound Transit that this additional travel time isn’t acceptable. So when planning the 2026 ST Express network, Sound Transit decided to keep buses when travel times by cutting them would exceed 10 minutes (per The Urbanist , reporting from Sound Transit’s Director of System and Service Planning, Emily Yasukochi).

In keeping with the feedback they received, Sound Transit’s eventual plan had routes 545 and 542 in the “no changes” column. Here are the resulting service frequencies as they took effect late last month:

During the week, riders will continue to have frequent service on route 545, but riders heading to UW or farther north opting to use the 542 will have no frequent service at any time. Missing a 542 could make taking the 2 Line all the around through Bellevue, Mercer Island, and downtown Seattle be a faster way to get to UW just because of the 30 minute wait. Worse yet, neither the 542 or 545 are frequent on weekends, making riders who have a faster trip have to decide between a fast but infrequent bus, or a frequent but circuitous train. By comparison, route 556 (which replaces route 554 and connects Issaquah to the 2 Line) sees frequent service every day of the week, and is also more usable for intra-eastside trips (e.g., Issaquah to Bellevue or Redmond) than route 554 was.

As part of its reporting on its proposals in the 2026 service plan, Sound Transit did an analysis of travel times on routes which were to be modified in 2026. Below is its analysis, which includes some popular trips which were made on routes 522, 550, 554, 556, 574, and 586 before the 2026 changes. They estimated travel times on these trips before the 2026 service changes (labeled “current”), and did the same estimate for travel times after the service changes (labeled “future”), under the new network. The final column gives an estimated additional travel time for each trip after the 2026 changes, with negative values indicating a quicker trip.
Per the rest of the document, these estimates are calculated by adding:

With Sound Transit being selective about which changes were made, it’s unsurprising that most of these trips saw a travel time decrease, with only Issaquah TC- downtown Seattle being slower in every case. More to the point, in all cases but one, additional travel time is less than the 10 minute threshold Sound Transit set for planning bus changes to new Link service.

Because Sound Transit did not make changes to route 545, they did not provide their travel time analysis. I suspect they analyzed trips on route 545 against the same trips on the Link 2 Line, as all trips between Redmond and Seattle on routes 545 map decently well to a single 2 Line trip. However, assuming route 545 is cut and service is added to route 542 (as proposed in 2021), a frequent route 542 with a transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW could also approximate any route 545 trip. Below is an analysis I did of six trips on route 545, using the same method Sound Transit used to calculate the other changes:

Trip A: Downtown Redmond to International District/Chinatown Station Trip B: Downtown Redmond to Westlake Station Trip C: Redmond Technology Station to International District/Chinatown Station Trip D: Redmond Technology Station to Westlake Station Trip E: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to International District/Chinatown Station Trip F: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to Westlake Station

To easily see the impact of the changes, I’ve colored cells red if times are more than 10 minutes longer, green if more than 5 minutes shorter, a shade of yellow if less than 10 minutes longer, and a shade of blue of less than 5 minutes shorter. I’ve also marked 2 Line-only travel times in italics , and 542 + 1/2 Line travel times in bold .

From the results, I think Sound Transit only analyzed the travel time impact of 2 Line-only trips, and did not consider 542 + 1/2 Line at all. Because while (to my surprise) the 2 Line competes with route 545 very well on most trips, the directness of route 545 to Redmond Technology Station makes those trips impossible to match on the 2 Line, with an added delay of 20 minutes in the worst case. But when you add in the option to take the more frequent 542 and transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW, this adds a faster option in the exact cases where the single 2 Line trip fares the worst against the 545. In fact, when this option is added, every case has an alternative to its route 545 trip that adds less delay than the 10 minute planning threshold Sound Transit uses, with most trips getting faster (with the most improved trip being 25 minutes faster from Marymoor to IDS).

Lastly, one thing this analysis doesn’t account for is something that you often see on route 545 toward Seattle on weekday afternoons, which are catastrophic delays. In particular, the turn from Stewart St to 5th Ave often gets so congested that route 545 buses often wait 10-20 minutes just to make this one turn. If the travel time analysis of alternative options wasn’t reason enough to move route 545 service hours elsewhere, the fact that Sound Transit is predictably wasting a large amount of service hours just waiting for this one turn just underscores how route 545 needs a second look.

If route 545 were to be deleted, this would free up a ton of service hours. Obviously the first priority would be to boost route 542 frequencies to 10 minutes peak/15 minutes midday, and extend it to Bear Creek P&R via Downtown Redmond Station (taking over the 545’s eastern section). I also think route 542 should be increased to every 15 minutes on weekends as well (something which actually wasn’t proposed in 2021 , as it kept the 542 every 30 minutes on weekends). Since half of this route 542 service already exist, this would only use up significantly less than half of route 545’s service hours.

The next priority could be restoring route 544 to South Lake Union. This was a route that Sound Transit created in March 2020 following a restructure that consolidated some service from Kirkland and Redmond to create a new route serving an emerging market for commuter service to SLU. However, being started at the beginning of the pandemic, it only operated a couple weeks before it was suspended . Originally, it proposed to be restored in 2021 as part of East Link Connections. I think this is a good idea, though I also think some changes should be made. King County Metro has shown it can run buses from SR 520 to the Mercer St exit today (something which was long though to be impossible in regular service) on route 256. Furthermore, WSDOT is planning to open a direct express lane connection between this exit and SR 520 for transit in the 2030s. So I think a restored 544 should exit at Mercer St, and could lay over at the bus layover area on Eastlake.

On the eastside, it’s also worth reevaluating whether it makes sense to run the 544 to the Overlake P&R, or even to Redmond at all. If a shorter route 544 could be made more frequent, it could facilitate 2-seat rides if moved to the right places. The way I think it could maximize connection opportunities is to serve S. Kirkland P&R, then terminate at Spring District Station, with frequencies of 8 minutes. This allows connections from routes 542 and 270 at the 520 freeway stations, some Kirkland routes at S. Kirkland, and the 2 Line at Spring District (and transfers would work well from both the east and south here).

Whether the remaining service hours after changes to the 542 go into restoring route 544 or something else entirely, what will be the case is that, while not every rider will have a faster trip, many riders will, and all riders will enjoy more frequent and consistent service across every day of the week. When express buses complement rail rather than competing with it, then both services will work better for more riders.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Dan Strauss invited Sound Transit board members, city officials, and state officials to a Ballard Link Extension (BLE) Community Forum Monday to provide the public with information on the Ballard Link extension plans. The Nordic Museum’s auditorium was packed with residents from Ballard and along the route as well as from the Eastside and even Tacoma. After short opening remarks from the officials, Sound Transit CEO Constantine introduced Brad Owen (acting Chief Delivery Officer, former Los Angeles Metro), Lauren Matthias (who joined the BLE team as Project Director from Vancouver’s Broadway SkyTrain) and Dan Turner (long time BLE Project Manager). Then Dan Strauss took questions from the audience.

While many aspects were discussed, it became clear that Sound Transit does not envision any major changes but is focusing on reducing the cost of the project as envisioned. They are hoping Olympia will enact increasing debt allowance (by borrowing for 75 years instead of 40, which effectively reduces debt burden by $1b) and a better federal funding environment (faster grants).

Brad Owen pointed out that they already reduced the West Seattle Link Extension (WSLE) cost by $2b (after the cost had quadrupled). He said that they have already identified potential savings of $1-3b for BLE (such as a smaller trapezoidal Seattle Center station). They have just concluded an industry request for information (RFI). Some suggestions (from Alstrom, contractors, and others) had already been incorporated; others will be. In order to deliver BLE by 2042, they need to shed about $10b, otherwise it may take longer. The audience voiced concerns whether more stations would get dropped (such as Avalon and South Lake Union), and asked why WSLE was prioritized over BLE when estimates for BLE ridership are four times as high. Brad Owen pointed out that projects usually get phased in (such as L.A.’s Purple Line) and WSLE was approved first.

ST has studied automated trains. As those could not interoperate with the Rainier Line, it could only work from Ballard to Westlake and would require different trains and a separate maintenance facility. They don’t think the existing tunnel can be tapped safely to reach the existing SODO maintenance center. They would lose the regional funding (49%) currently committed for the second downtown tunnel. Brad Owen said: “In order to introduce new trains, you have to isolate the line, meaning Ballard to West Seattle, not the line extension, as it’s currently planned… Even with $2b savings for station size, we would introduce less capacity to the system and need new fleet and maintenance upgrades. It won’t actually reduce cost. We have already started to reduce the station size such as in Alaska Junction station.”

They have not studied an elevated alternative as it would require that they start the project from scratch (new scoping document). Downtown is too tight for big guideways to meet NEPA requirements (such as fire code) and would require too much utility relocations and disturbance.

While transit riders wait for BLE, somebody asked for Metro/SDOT to provide some mitigation until the line becomes available. The mayor promised to look into adding more bus lanes and discuss service improvements with Metro. Dan Strauss pointed out that express lines were cancelled during Covid and are still not reestablished. It will be important to get the Seattle Transit Measure passed and then work with Metro. KCC Baron mentioned that Metro will start a major restructure next year.
Dan Strauss reaffirmed to the audience that failure is not an option.

articles.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
articles.author: Lizz Giordano
paras: Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.
As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.
The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.
“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.
In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
